What You Need to Run MadMapper

MadMapper is designed to be lightweight, flexible, and compatible with a wide range of hardware configurations.

Whether you’re working on a small projection mapping project or a large-scale installation, here’s what you need to know about supported systems and recommended setups.

 

At its core, all you need to get started with MadMapper is a computer running macOS or Windows

Also meaning even with the Demo version you can explore the interface, design your mappings, and experiment with ideas entirely on-screen.

 

The minimum hardware requirements to run MadMapper is a computer running macOS or Windows

At least 300 MB of disk space and a minimum of 2 GB of RAM and a GPU compatible with OpenGL 3.3.

 

We recommend a CPU with at least 2–4 cores and a minimum of 8 GB of RAM. An SSD and a dedicated GPU are also highly recommended for optimal performance.

 

MadMapper 6 runs seamlessly on both macOS and Windows, offering the same powerful performances and features across platforms.

macOS: version 11 or higher

Windows: version 10 or higher

 

There is no “better” platform, both systems are fully supported and deliver excellent performance.

 

Your choice will mostly come down to personal preference, budget, and the kind of projects you plan to create. Some artists prefer macOS for its streamlined workflow and system stability, while others choose Windows for its flexibility and broader hardware options.

 

Ultimately, both platforms let you get the most out of MadMapper’s creative potential. 

macOS Recommendations

MadMapper performs well even on modest Apple hardware, making it an excellent choice for portability and reliability.

  • Entry-Level: Standard MacBooks (such as the MacBook Air or older MacBook Pro models) are perfectly fine for common projection mapping tasks. Even a second-hand MacBook can be suitable for light to medium use.

  • Heavy Workloads: If you plan to work extensively with heavy shaders, multiple high-resolution video inputs, or large 3D content, you will benefit significantly from a more powerful GPU.

  • Apple Silicon: MadMapper has been written as a native M-software for Apple Silicon (M-series) computers since version 5, ensuring maximum efficiency on modern Macs.

MadMapper has been a native M-software for Apple Silicon (M-series) computers since version 5.

Windows Recommendations

MadMapper runs equally well on Windows systems, provided they are properly configured. Even compact PCs such as Intel NUCs or mini PCs can handle projection mapping surprisingly well, making them ideal for small or portable permanent installations.

  • Processor (CPU): Choose a recent, high-performance model (such as an Intel i5/i7/i9 or AMD Ryzen series). Avoid entry-level CPUs, which can easily bottleneck your performance.

  • Storage: An SSD drive is strongly recommended to ensure fast project loading and smooth video playback.

  • Memory (RAM): At least 8 GB is required, though 16 GB or more is highly recommended for smooth performance when juggling multiple media files.

  • Graphics Card (GPU): A dedicated GPU is essential for heavy video, LED, and laser workloads. Both NVIDIA and AMD cards are fully supported.

    • NVIDIA Driver Recommendation: It is strongly advised to install the NVIDIA Studio Driver rather than the standard "Game Ready" driver. The Studio driver prioritizes absolute stability for creative applications, whereas the Game Ready driver contains game-specific optimization tricks that are unnecessary for MadMapper and can occasionally introduce instability in live environments.

    • Display Stability Note: The most common hardware-related crashes on Windows occur when physically disconnecting or reconnecting displays while the GPU is actively under load. To ensure absolute stability, always physically connect and configure your display outputs before launching MadMapper.

Once installed, launch MadMapper and you will first encounter the MadMapper Authorization Manager.

At this step, you can choose to authorize MadMapper or its extensions.

You’ll also find information about the computer on which the software will be used.

Select License(s)

Next, select the license you want to use on this computer.

This step displays all your available licenses, including the number of computers already authorized, the license version(s), and their serial numbers.

You can also click the Manage button to access the Licenses tab in your user account on the website.

As noted above, temporary licenses can be stored for activation and use at a later time.

 

The following steps follow the same process and will only appear if you have chosen one or more extensions to authorize:

Validation

The next step confirms what will be authorized on this computer:

By clicking on Proceed, you'll have to enter your computer’s session password (not your MadMapper login), and you’ll reach the final step: restarting MadMapper fully authorized.

And then, it's showtime !

Update MadMapper

You do not need to log out your license before installing a MadMapper update on the same computer.

 

Updates are checked automatically, and if a new version is available you will be notified when you open MadMapper.

Once the installation file for the latest version has been downloaded, you can begin the installation process.

If you install a MadMapper update, it will not replace previous versions of MadMapper already installed on your computer.

You can have multiple different versions of MadMapper installed on your computer.

Deauthorize MadMapper

Logout From MadMapper

Directly from MadMapper, go to the Account menu at the top of the software/screen > Manage Authorizations:

 

 

Choose whether you want to deauthorize (log out) MadMapper and/or its extensions, then follow the steps in the Authorization Manager as you did when activating the software:

You have the flexibility to deauthorize the software or its extensions on one computer to authorize them on another whenever needed, with no restrictions on the number of times you can switch between devices.

You must also deauthorize MadMapper in the following cases:

- Formatting or erasing a computer
- Activating MadMapper on a new computer if all seats are already in use

Online Reset

If you no longer have access to a computer you need to deauthorize, you can revoke its authorization remotely using a Reset operation.

As the Reset operation is an emergency procedure, its use is limited: if you use a Reset token for one of your licenses, you'll have to wait a year to get your Reset token back for that license.

You can recover a Reset token by launching MadMapper on the computer for which you used the Reset operation.

The MadLaser and MadProjector extensions do not have dedicated installation files, they require MadMapper to be installed and the extensions to be authorized.

You can authorize or deauthorize (log in or log out) extensions at any time using the Authorization Manager.

As a reminder, you cannot use MadLaser or MadProjectorControl as standalone applications.

You must own a MadMapper license, either temporary or perpetual.

The installation process for the MadMapper Demo version is identical to that of the full version.

Mass Deploy Script

Use the script below to deploy remote activations.

 
- Authorisation example:
Mac: sudo /Applications/MadMapper\ 6.0.0.app/Contents/MacOS/MadMapper --authorise --serial=AAAA-BBBB-CCCC-DDDD-EEEE --username=myAccount --password=myPassword
Windows: C:\Program Files\MadMapper 6.0.0> .\MadMapper.exe --authorise --serial=AAAA-BBBB-CCCC-DDDD-EEEE --username=myAccount --password=myPassword

- Deauthorisation example:
Mac: sudo /Applications/MadMapper\ 6.0.0.app/Contents/MacOS/MadMapper --deauthorise --product=MadMapper
Windows: C:\Program Files\MadMapper 6.0.0> .\MadMapper.exe --deauthorise --product=MadMapper

- Login user to the Library
Mac: /Applications/MadMapper\ 6.0.0.app/Contents/MacOS/MadMapper --login --username=myUsername --password=myPassword
Windows: C:\Program Files\MadMapper 6.0.0> .\MadMapper.exe --login --username=myUsername --password=myPassword

- List products & authorisations:
Mac: /Applications/MadMapper\ 6.0.0.app/Contents/MacOS/MadMapper --authInfo
Windows: C:\Program Files\MadMapper 6.0.0> .\MadMapper.exe --authInfo

- Remark: on Windows, the application's log doesn't appear in the terminal, but the log-files are located there:
C:\Users\your_login\AppData\Roaming\Garagecube\MadMapper\Logs\

The sudo usage in the examples is used to allow MadMapper to write authorisation files to the filesystem, it's accessible to all users on the system.

“6.0.0.” is an example. Be sure to replace it with the actual version you are using whenever the version is mentioned.

Laser Surfaces

Arming the Laser & Output Preparation

While you can design and preview your laser surfaces within the software workspace, no physical light will be emitted from your hardware until the system is armed.

To see your image in the real world, you must arm the laser by toggling the Laser Output icon located in the upper right corner of the main MadMapper application window.

 

Crucial Pre-Flight Check: Before arming the laser, it is highly recommended that you configure and enable any necessary area limitations or "safety masks" within the Laser Output menu to physically block beams from hitting unsafe areas. (Note: A detailed breakdown of projector-specific safety zones and hardware routing will be covered in the separate Outputs documentation page).

 

The Arming Warning The first time you arm the laser output during a session, MadMapper will present a mandatory safety acknowledgment:

Please read this carefully. As the software explicitly states:

  • Lasers are powerful and dangerous, hence they should be handled with care and safety for the audience in mind.

  • Please comply with your local regulations.

Once you accept the prompt and the laser icon is activated, MadMapper will begin sending live vector data to your connected hardware.

Basics

Laser surfaces allow you to create and manage your laser outputs for your mapping projects. By adding laser surfaces, you define how shapes, generative content, or video textures are translated into real-time laser trajectories on your physical installation.

Unlike standard video projection, MadMapper handles laser content in two distinct ways:

  • Native Laser Materials: Generative, shader-based materials (GLSL) that natively output mathematical vector data directly to the laser hardware. This circumvents the need for pixel-tracing, resulting in the sharpest, most scanner-efficient rendering possible.

  • Image Vectorization (Tracing): A GPU-accelerated, custom OpenCV engine that analyzes pixel-based media in real time. This allows you to trace contours and paths from movies, live camera inputs, or by sampling directly from your active video composition.

Laser Surface Types

Laser Quad

This allows you to map vector graphics or vectorize video content within a four-point warped surface similar to a Video surface:

 

Laser Lines

It allows you to create precise, path-based line surfaces, perfect for tracing physical architecture. The drawing behavior changes based on your input:

  • Straight Lines: Select the Laser Line tool, then click points on the Output Stage to draw sharp angles. Press Return or Esc to finish the path.

  • Bezier Curves: Click and drag on the Output Stage to draw free-form, curved lines. Once you release the mouse, MadMapper will automatically simplify the stroke into adjustable anchor points.

  • Adding Points: To add a new anchor point to an existing line, simply double-click anywhere on the path.

Advanced Point Editing Once a line is created, you can right-click any specific anchor point to access a context menu for advanced path editing. The available options adapt based on the type of point selected:

  • Continue Path from Here (C): Resumes drawing the line starting from the selected end point.

  • Enable / Disable Bezier (B): Toggles the selected point between a sharp, rigid corner and a smooth, curved point.

  • Split Path Here (S): Breaks a single, continuous line into two entirely separate line segments at the selected point.

  • Link Tangents (L): (Available only on Bezier points) Locks the two Bezier handles together so that adjusting the curve on one side perfectly mirrors the other. Unlinking them allows you to adjust each side independently for sharp, customized curves.

   

Tip: Similar to standard vector drawing software, whenever you select a point with Bezier enabled, two directional handles will appear. Click and drag these handles to precisely adjust the arc and trajectory of your laser curve.

Laser Circle

Add circles as a laser surface, then adjust (with the four handle points), scale, and rotate your circle(s) directly in the Stage View. Just like with video surfaces, the perspective can be scaled using the center handle. This surface type is ideal for mapping rounded architectural elements or generating geometric tunnel effects:

 

Laser Text

Create sharp, legible text that is natively generated as laser-optimized vector paths, including support for single-line stick fonts. (See the Laser Surface Inspector below for more details on text formatting).

Laser 3D

Import and calibrate 3D objects in the .OBJ format directly to your laser output. This surface type allows you to import standard .OBJ files and project them as high-definition volumetric wireframes: (See the 3D Surface Inspector below for more details).

Laser Surface Inspectors

The Laser Surface Inspector, located below the list of surfaces, displays the settings and parameters of the selected surface (highlighted in the surfaces list). The available settings vary depending on the specific type of Laser surface you are working with.

Media, Appearance, FX, and Output

For these standard formatting and routing parameters, please refer to the general settings detailed in the Video Surfaces Documentation. They behave identically across both video and laser workflows.

 

Laser Render

 

Advanced controls dictating how the software translates visual data into physical scanner movements:

  • Scan & Beam Mode: Set to Auto or manually configure.

  • Max Speed: Defines the maximum drawing speed of the laser.

  • Optimize Angles: When activated, utilizes the Angle Min, Angle Delay, and End Repeat parameters to instruct the laser scanners to dwell slightly on sharp corners, ensuring crisp geometry instead of rounded edges.

  • In Fade / Out Fade / Soft Close: Controls the blanking (turning the laser diode on/off) at the start and end of drawing paths to prevent visible tails or connecting lines.

Process

(Applies only to Laser Quads, Circles, and 3D Objects) Dictates how content is vectorized into laser paths. The options change based on the surface type:

(Image for Quads/Circles)  (Image for 3D)

 

  • For Quads & Circles: Controls real-time image tracing. Set the Mode (e.g., Find Paths), adjust the tracing Threshold, toggle Use Color, and refine the trace using Thickness, Denoizing, and Max Res to balance detail against scanner workload.

  • For 3D Objects: Controls volumetric rendering. Set the Mode (e.g., Depth), and fine-tune the Sensibility and Definition to control how much geometric wireframe detail is sent to the laser.

Path Filtering

(Applies only to Laser Quads, Circles, and 3D Objects) Allows you to filter out unwanted geometry based on physical length:

  • Min / Max Length: Defines the length limits as a percentage of the media dimension. For example, setting Min Length to 10% on a 1024x1024 video will automatically hide any generated polylines that are shorter than roughly 11 pixels, which is excellent for instantly removing visual noise from traced video.

Path Limits

(Applies only to Laser Quads, Circles, and 3D Objects) A critical safety and optimization tool to prevent overwhelming the laser scanners with too much complex geometry:

  • Count: Defines the absolute maximum number of polylines to keep and send to the laser. (Pro-tip: Press the Option (Mac) / Alt (PC) key while dragging the slider for fine-tuning).

  • Mode: If the vectorization exceeds the maximum Count limit, this parameter defines which paths to prioritize and keep (e.g., Keep Longest or Keep Shortest).

Mesh Warping

(Applies only to Laser Quads, Lines, and Text) An essential technique that applies a grid mesh to warp your laser output. Activate Bezier Mesh Warping to use curves to fit your laser perfectly to complex physical surfaces. (See Video Mesh Warping for more details).

Soft-Edge

(Applies only to Laser Quads) Extremely useful when overlapping multiple laser projectors. This allows you to blend and fade the intersecting laser zones smoothly. (See Video Mesh Warping for more details).

 

Note: If you Shift + Select multiple surfaces at once, the Inspector will only display the common parameters shared by all selected surfaces. Additionally, remember that the percentage of a setting on an individual surface is always multiplied by the master settings of its parent Group.

Laser Text Settings

When a Laser Text surface is selected, this dedicated panel appears for typographic control:

  • Text Box & Aspect Ratio: Type your characters and define the overall proportions of the text's bounding box on the output stage.

  • Font Type & Font: Choose your typeface. You can select standard system fonts, or switch to Stick Font. (Tip: Stick Fonts are highly recommended for laser use, as they trace a single line to reduce scanner flicker).

  • Formatting: Adjust italics, horizontal/vertical alignment, and reading direction.

  • Adjust Font Size To Fit: Automatically scale your typography to perfectly fill the defined bounding box.

Laser Lines Settings

When a Laser Lines surface is selected, access tools for managing your custom vector paths (similar to Video Lines):

  • Tools & Layers: Manage, select, and organize the individual line segments drawn within the surface.

  • Min Points: Defines the minimum number of ILDA points to generate for the selected path. (Pro-tip: Press the Option (Mac) / Alt (PC) key while dragging the slider for fine-tuning).

  • Revert Path / SVG IO: Quickly revert edits, or use Import/Export SVG to load external vector artwork or save your custom stage traces.

Laser 3D Settings

When a Laser 3D surface is selected, access tools for projecting volumetric shapes (Similar to Video 3D surfaces):

  • 3D Model: Select a built-in primitive shape (like a Box) or import your own .OBJ file. Adjust Face Culling to hide the back sides of objects, drastically optimizing laser rendering.

  • Texturing: Define how textures and colors map to the Object UVs.

  • Calibration: Use the Calibrate toggle and Fix Position button to accurately align the 3D rendering with real-world physical objects.

Display

Specifies what is visually rendered in the software preview. This is an essential diagnostic tool used for understanding the internal vectorization process and figuring out how your source media creation or encoding can be improved for better laser output.

  • Mode: Use the dropdown to switch the workspace preview between different stages of the rendering pipeline. Options include:

    • Output Polylines: Displays the final, generated vector paths that will be sent to the physical laser.

    • Normals / Depth / Color: Visualizes specific data channels extracted from the source media.

    • Processed Image / Thinned Image: Shows the intermediate steps of the computer vision engine as it breaks down standard video pixels into traceable lines.

Monitor

 

Displays real-time errors and statistical information about the vectorization process. Use this panel to keep an eye on the internal math (like Initial Polyline Count vs. Recomposed Polylines) to ensure your composition isn't generating an unsafe or overwhelming amount of geometry for the hardware scanners to process.

Advanced Laser Preferences For global hardware routing (such as AVB/Dante audio-to-laser networks) and critical project safety limits (including non-moving beam intensity and Expert Mode scan rates), please refer to the laser-specific settings detailed in the MadLaser Preferences documentation.

 

Expert Mode Surface Features

When Expert Mode is enabled in your Project Preferences, the Laser Surface inspector unlocks several advanced, under-the-hood parameters designed for complex installations and high-end hardware.

  • RGB Samples (Laser Lines & Text): Increases the maximum allowable color sampling resolution up to 64k (default is 8k). Warning: 64k samples will have a heavy impact on software performance.

  • Expanded Speed Ranges: Increases the maximum allowed values for the Max Speed and Fixed Speed parameters up to 5.0 (normally restricted to 3.0 to protect entry-level scanners).

  • Start Repeat: Unhides a dedicated parameter allowing you to add extra dwell points specifically at the starting point of a path.

  • Advanced Video Vectorization: Unlocks deeper, experimental variables when converting standard video or images into laser paths (using "Find Paths" or "Find Contours").

  • Maximum Input Dimension: Allows the video vectorization engine to process media up to 16k resolution (normally limited to 8k). While real-time performance may degrade at 16k, this is an incredibly powerful feature for converting massive files into non-real-time ILDA exports via the Timeline.

You are strictly responsible for complying with all local, regional, and national laser safety laws in your country (such as FDA variance reporting in the US, or equivalent local regulations). Always ensure beam paths are safely terminated, account for unpredictable live event variables like moving performers, and never operate without appropriate hardware safety monitoring systems engaged. Use at your own risk.

Laser Drawing Order and Optimization

Does the layer order of Laser Surfaces determine their drawing order? No. Unlike video surfaces where the layer stack determines what is rendered on top, the Laser Output receives all paths from all active laser surfaces simultaneously. The software then mathematically calculates the most efficient rendering order to optimize "blanking time" and minimize the physical distance the scanner needs to travel. This ensures the fastest, cleanest global scan possible.

DMX: Import / Export from SVG

MadMapper 6.1 comes with Bézier Fixtures which allows new possibilities for importing fixtures from SVG. While MadMapper 5 was only import "line" elements from SVG, MadMapper 6.1 can load "line","rect","circle","ellipse","polygon","polyline","path".

 

Also in MadMapper 6.1 a fixture definition can be set to LED Strip mode or LED Matrix mode. In this case, you can specify the strip length (or matrix size) for each fixture. So if you have a strip with 160 pixels, one with 165, one with 100 pixels, they can all use the Fixture Definition « LED Strip RGB » and you specify the size for each Fixture. Same for matrices.

 

We've also added options to specify fixtures parameters directly your your vector file editor (ie Illustrator, Inkscape etc.). For instance DMX patching (universe / channel) can be specified from the layer "id" exported in SVG file. It is also possible to generate an SVG from a script or with an AI and add DMX patching info as XML tags of the geometry elements in the SVG.

Another improvement : when imported from SVG, layer groups in the SVG will generate fixture groups in MadMapper, it will respect and reproduce the hierarchy.

 

Exporting fixtures to SVG and importing it in a new project will recreate the original setup (fixture types, geometry, line/circle thickness, DMX patching (universe / channel), group hierarchy etc. This make new workflows easy:

  • Create fixture setup in MadMapper, export as SVG and use it in a software like After Effects to create a video animation easiely that will perfectly match fixtures.
  • Create fixture setup in an SVG file from a vector editor (Illustrator) or with an AI and import it, it can also be used in a video editing software to create content.

This document describes how an SVG file will be interpreted by MadMapper when using File / Import Fixtures and choosing an SVG file (CSV import has not been modified).

Additional settings extracted from "id"

The id of a layer can include all necessary parameters to create the fixtures. If the layer id is « MySuperLedStrip », it will just create a fixture with name «  MySuperLedStrip » (fixture type will be deduced from svg geometry type : line, rect etc.).

 

But the id can include extra info. For instance if the id is « MySuperLedStrip__UN__10__CH__12 », the fixture name will be « MySuperLedStrip » and MadMapper will set UNiverse to 10 and CNannel to 12.

Supported data

- « __UN__ » : Universe number (0-32767)

- « __CH__ » : Channel number (1-512)

- « __FT__ » : Fixture Type to create. Possible values : « fixture_bezier », « fixture_line », « fixture_circle », « fixture_quad »

- « __FD__ » : Fixture Definition, for instance « Generic – Pixel RGB » or « GarageCube - SFX-01 W 1m » (Group[space]-[space]Name)

- « __SL__ » : Strip Length (for fixture definition set to LED Strip mode)

- « __MW__ » and « __MH__ » : Matrix Width / Height (for fixture definition set to Matrix mode)

- « __TH__ » : Thickness in pixels of the line & bezier, or thickness pourcentage for circle fixture

Additional settings in XML elements

This data can also be added as attributes of the geometry XML element if editing from a text editor / script or with an AI, it avoid having very long and cryptic Ids:

- « universe » : Universe number (0-32767)

- « channel » : Channel number (1-512)

- « fixture_type » : Fixture Type to create. Possible values : « fixture_bezier », « fixture_line », « fixture_circle », « fixture_quad »

- « fixture_definition » : Fixture Definition, for instance « Generic – Pixel RGB » or « GarageCube - SFX-01 W 1m » (Group[space]-[space]Name)

- « strip_length » : Strip Length (for fixture definition set to LED Strip mode)

- « matrix_width » and « matrix_height » : Matrix Width / Height (for fixture definition set to Matrix mode)

- « thickness » : Thickness in pixels of the line & bezier, or thickness pourcentage for circle fixture

What fixture type will be created

- If « fixture_type » (« __FT__ ») is specified, MadMapper will create a fixture of the chosen type (refer to previous section)

- If the SVG geometry element is a « line » MadMapper will create an « Fixture Line » surface

- If the SVG geometry element is a « rect » and is not rounded (with rx & ry), MadMapper will create an « Fixture Quad » surface

- For any other type it will create a « Fixture Bezier »

Extensions & Companions

To expand the core capabilities of the software, the MadMapper ecosystem includes specialized extensions and companion hardware designed for specific professional workflows:

MadLaser

 

MadLaser is an extension of MadMapper dedicated to laser mapping. Compatible with multiple laser hardware devices, MadLaser transforms any shape, text, or generative content into laser trajectories in real time. Create fluid, sharp, and expressive animations directly synchronized with video, audio, or lighting.

MadLaser Key Features

  • Unlimited laser outputs: As many as your computer can handle
  • Multi Hardware supported: Ether Dream, ShowNET, Helios, FB3, FB4 (with Pangolin and Windows), AVB/Dante, LaserCube, IDN
  • Laser Bezier lines: Ultra-precise vector graphics
  • 3D object rendering from .OBJ format

  • Real-Time Video Vectorization: Hardware-accelerated image analysis and processing.

  • Vector Materials: Real-time, shader-based generative laser content.

  • High-Speed Scanning: Supports up to 100 kpps scanners for high-definition graphics.

  • Advanced Routing: Laser Soft Edge on quads, and Laser Dispatch to spread complex content across multiple projectors.

  • Visualization & Safety: Robust pre-visualization capabilities and critical safety zoning.

  • ILDA Support: Import and export standard ILDA files.

MadLaser is an extension of MadMapper and cannot operate as a standalone application.

A MadMapper license is required.

MadProjectorControl

 

The MadProjectorControl extension uses the PJLink protocol to remotely control any number of compatible video projectors. Fully cueable, this extension allows you to schedule and automate power and shutter activity directly from your mapping station.

 

Main features:

  • Compatible with any PJLink-compliant device.

  • Control and monitor an unlimited number of projectors.

  • Cueable, schedulable, and automatable.

  • Remote Power On/Off and Shutter control.

  • Displays live device information and lamp status.

Like MadLaser, MadProjectorControl is an extension and requires a MadMapper license.

MadAI

 

Transform ideas into dynamic visuals without writing a single line of code. Whether you need material (shader) generation, 2D effects, or laser animations, simply type a prompt and MadAI will take care of the rest. You can also use AI to remix existing content from your library to find new inspiration.

MiniMad

 

MiniMad is a hardware plug-and-play device designed to play back your MadMapper setups with automatic network synchronization for multi-projection, or DMX/Art-Net output to control lighting and LED equipment.

 

MiniMad makes your installation easy and affordable: it hooks up to a projector and plays content on surfaces exported from MadMapper. Alternatively, you can achieve an equivalent outcome through light mapping. Small by size but feature-rich, the MiniMad allows you to export quad, triangle, circle, or mask surfaces as well as their content from a selected projector in MadMapper. You can also switch the MiniMad to lighting mode and output DMX/Art-Net channel data to your light fixtures.

 

Discreet and Autonomous

The MiniMad can run on its own for a very long time—units in the lab have run continuously for more than a year. In case of a power failure, the MiniMad automatically restarts without any user intervention. All the mapping modifications you do are automatically saved on the SD card.

 

Team Power

Multiple MiniMads can be synchronized with each other over Ethernet to make a cluster of synchronized video players. Zero configuration is needed; MadMapper will automatically split movies and optimize files for playback.

 

MiniMad Main Features

  • Automatic synchronization of video media playback when multiple MiniMads are connected to the same Ethernet network.

  • In-depth quality export with precise video controls.

  • Up to 64 universes for Art-Net/DMX.

  • Autonomous playback of content recorded from MadMapper.

  • Multi-channel audio when using Light mode.

  • Native video playback up to 1080p30 in optimal conditions.

  • Physical controls with friendly buttons to tweak your mapping directly on location.

  • Video or Light: 2 playback modes available.

  • VideoWall easy setup—a one-click, fully automated process.

  • Zero configuration, as simple as that.

  • Playback modes: loop, random, list... configure your MiniMad to play back your videos exactly the way you want.

  • Mesh Warping and Perspective Pinning with adjustable manual controls.

  • Remote control your MiniMads directly from MadMapper.

 

Technical Specifications

  • Raspberry Pi 2
  • 7 buttons control panel
  • 1x HDMI output up to 1080p (1920x1080 at 60Hz)
  • Size: 9 x 6 x 3 cm (approx. 3.5 x 2.3 x 1.2 inches)

  • MiniMad is setup for either video mapping or light mapping; it cannot do both at the same time. Use different units to do so.

  • Media playback (video) is automatically synced when MiniMad units are connected to the same Ethernet network. This can induce a one-frame delay between the different units. Therefore the device is not suitable for blending/soft-edge.

  • For MiniMads that are running continuously for months, i.e., for an installation, we recommend using industrial-grade Micro SD cards as well as having backup SD cards with your project already exported.

The Outputs Tab

The Outputs tab represents the final stage of your MadMapper pipeline. This is where your digital workspace is translated and routed to physical hardware or virtual destinations. It provides comprehensive tools for managing multi-projector setups, configuring laser routing, establishing global safety masks, and creating off-screen buffers.

Note: You can quickly access the Outputs tab using the keyboard shortcut Cmd + 5 on macOS or Ctrl + 5 on Windows.

Creating & Managing Outputs

At the top of the Outputs list, you can define the physical or virtual hardware that MadMapper will communicate with.

  • Video Output: Add standard video outputs for connected displays, projectors, or LED wall processors.

  • Laser Output: Configure dedicated routes to your ILDA laser DACs (Digital-to-Analog Converters) or network-based laser controllers.

  • DMX Output: Set up universes and network protocols (such as Art-Net or sACN) for your patched lighting fixtures and pixel-mapped LED tape.

  • Buffers: Create off-screen rendering targets (Video or Laser) to composite and manipulate content before sending it to a physical output.

Similar to other aspects of MadMapper, in this menu you can enable/disable outputs and lock/unlock them.

 

Warning: Disabling an active output during a show will immediately close its fullscreen projection.

Output Settings Reference Guide

When you select an output or buffer in the Outputs List, the settings panel at the bottom of the screen populates with specific parameters for that device. Below is a breakdown of the available settings for each output type.

Video Output Settings

These settings control how your digital canvas is routed to physical displays, projectors, or other software.

  • Destination: Select the physical display (e.g., Built-in Retina Display, connected projectors) or virtual destination. It displays hardware info such as GPU, Resolution, and Frequency.

  • Output Size: Define the exact pixel resolution (Width x Height). You can lock the aspect ratio or toggle fullscreen.

  • Flip: Quickly mirror the output horizontally, vertically, or both (essential for rear projection).

  • Delay: Add a frame delay to synchronize mixed hardware outputs.

  • Enable Antialiasing (MSAA): Smooths jagged edges on 3D geometry and masks.

  • Routing Buttons:

    • Desktop Window: Opens the output in a floating window.

    • Publish to Syphon / Spout: Sends the video output to other visual software on the same computer.

    • Publish to NDI: Broadcasts the video output over your local network.

    • Publish Internal Loopback: Routes the output back into MadMapper's Media Bin as a live source.

  • Show Test Pattern: Toggles a built-in test card for alignment.

  • Background & Mask: Load custom reference images or apply global masks, complete with adjustable Opacity sliders.

  • Save Video Snapshot: Captures the current frame of the output to a specified format (e.g., PNG 8 bits RGBA).

Laser Output Settings

MadMapper provides extensive hardware control for ILDA laser projectors to ensure safe and accurate rendering.

  • Destination: Select your connected laser DAC. MadMapper natively supports Etherdream, ShowNet, Helios USB, and Pangolin FB4.

  • Output Size & Flip: Defines the size of the output rectangle in the preview interface. Note: This does not affect the physical output data; it is strictly for positioning surfaces relatively in the UI.

  • Publishing & Dispatch:

    • Publish Internal Loopback: This powerful feature renders your laser composition into a new source in the Media List. This allows you to apply Mesh Warping to an entire complex laser composition at once on a secondary projector.

    • Publish to PONK: Broadcasts the laser data over the network using the PONK protocol.

  • Device:

    • PPS (Points Per Second): Set the scanning speed to match your hardware manufacturer's specifications. Warning: Setting a value over 45kpps generally does not improve quality and can overheat or damage your galvos.

    • Delay: Adjust synchronization.

  • ILDA Engine:

    • Desired FPS: The target frame rate. Rates under 35 FPS will produce noticeable flickering.

    • Point Count & ILDA FPS: MadMapper calculates the real scan rate based on this formula: ILDA FPS = PPS / Point Count.

    • Scan Area: Sets boundaries to prevent the beam from hitting the physical edge of the scanner. Note: Setting this value too low can cause the galvos to enter a security mode or cause damage. Listen to your scanner; the sound should remain smooth.

    • Blank Delay: The time the laser takes to shut off, move, and turn back on between drawn paths. Increase this if your projected shapes have unwanted connecting lines.

  • Masks:

    • Draw zones to protect cameras or audiences. Applying a mask at a lower Opacity (e.g., 10%) allows you to safely scan an audience by significantly decreasing the luminosity in that specific region. Includes tools to Invert Mask, Mask Beams Only, and apply Feathering.

  • Test Pattern: Toggles specifically designed for laser calibration: Enable Scan Area, Enable Geometry, Enable Name, Enable Color, and Enable Masks.

  • Color Calibration:

    • Color Levels: Master RGB output limits.

    • Min Voltage: Laser diodes have varying thresholds before producing light. Set this minimum level to ensure colors (like red) shut off completely when rendering dark greys.

    • Response: Fine-tune the linearity of the RGB diodes using customizable curve graphs.

    • Color Delay: Compensates for hardware lag between the XY galvo position and the RGB diode firing by offsetting the color channels in time.

  • Distortion: Correct physical projection warping using Level X and Level Y.

  • Recording: Options to Store Ilda Frame or Record Ilda Movie to your Workspace folder. The Movie Mode dropdown offers two capture methods:

    • Record at fixed frame rate: Captures at a consistent rate. Use this if you plan to play the file back inside MadMapper or other video software.

    • Record as ILDA stream: Captures the raw, variable-frame-rate point data. Use this if you are exporting the file to an SD card to be played back directly by laser hardware.

DMX Output Settings

Used for routing pixel-mapped data to lighting fixtures via Art-Net or sACN.

  • Output Size: Defines the coordinate space for the DMX output.

  • Definition: Choose to keep the resolution the Same as Output Size, or define a Custom X/Y resolution depending on your pixel-mapping needs.

  • Background & Opacity: Load a stage plot or CAD drawing to trace your fixture layout.

Video Buffer Settings

Buffers allow you to create intermediate, off-screen rendering targets that can be manipulated before being sent to a final physical output.

  • Output Size: Define the resolution of the buffer.

  • Enable Antialiasing (MSAA): Smooths the rendered geometry within the buffer.

  • Format: Select the exact pixel format and color bit-depth for the buffer. Options include:

    • 8-bit formats: PF_U8_BGRA, PF_U8_RGB, PF_U8_L, PF_U8_RG

    • 32-bit float formats: PF_F32_RGBA, PF_F32_RGB, PF_F32_R

    • 16-bit float formats: PF_F16_RGBA, PF_F16_RGB, PF_F16_R

  • Include Alpha channel: Toggle transparency support for the buffer.

  • Background & Opacity: Add a reference image to the buffer canvas.

  • Save Video Snapshot: Export a still image of the current buffer state.

Laser Buffer Settings

Similar to Video Buffers, these allow you to composite multiple laser generators or lines off-screen before routing them to physical DACs.

  • Output Size: Define the resolution bounds of the laser buffer.

  • Dispatch to [X] outputs: Automatically distribute the rendered laser paths across multiple connected laser projectors.

  • Masks: Apply masking directly to the buffer level.

  • Background & Opacity: Load reference images to guide your laser composition.

Destinations & Display Routing

Once an output is created, you configure its Destination. This determines exactly how the pixel data is mapped and modified before leaving the graphics card.

  • Matrix Splitting: Destinations allow you to easily split your canvas across multiple physical displays (for example, breaking a 4K output into a 2x2 matrix of 1080p outputs for a video wall controller).

  • Geometry Adjustments: You can precisely adjust the output size and position, or apply horizontal/vertical flips (useful for rear-projection setups).

  • Frame Delay: Add micro-delays to specific outputs to perfectly synchronize older projectors with newer, faster displays in a mixed hardware setup.

  • Loopbacks & External Routing: Configure virtual destinations to manage internal and external video routing. You can loop your output back into MadMapper as a new media source, or send it out to other software using protocols like Syphon (Mac), Spout (PC), or NDI.

Backgrounds & Scanning Integration

To assist with the physical alignment of your surfaces, you can load reference images directly into the Output workspace.

  • Custom Backgrounds: Set a static image or blueprint of your stage design as the output background to trace over.

  • Spatial & Laser Scanner Import: If you are using MadMapper's Spatial Scanner (for projectors) or Laser Scanner tools, you can import the generated structured-light scans directly into the background. This allows you to accurately map complex 3D architecture from the comfort of your computer screen, even if you are entirely offline.

MadMapper Preferences

The Preferences menu (Cmd + , on Mac / Ctrl + , on PC) dictates the foundational behavior of the software. MadMapper 6 splits these preferences into two distinct tabs: Application (global settings that affect the software overall) and Project (settings saved specifically to the .mad file you currently have open).

Application Tab

These settings govern how the MadMapper application behaves on your specific computer, regardless of which project file is open.

Startup

Configure the initial User Interface state upon launch. Options include Always Minimize at startup, enabling Silent Mode (which suppresses user prompts—highly recommended for permanent installations), and toggling the Open Project dialog at startup.

General

Manage your safety net and UI features.

  • AutoSave & Backups: Enable AutoSave and define its interval (in minutes), and set the maximum number of automatic Project Backups.

  • Master: Choose whether to Reset Master settings on new project.

  • User Interface: Toggle Enable Expert Mode to expose advanced routing and programming features throughout the software.

  • MadAI: Enable Update Resource Thumbnail on Edition to automatically refresh generated previews.

Devices

The control center for external hardware inputs.

  • Video Input: Automatically check for connected devices, and enable native support for Blackmagic capture cards (including options to show all system-compliant devices and display outdated driver warnings), Canon EDSDK cameras, Kinect ONE depth sensors, and Intel RealSense.

  • Controls: Toggle support for external control peripherals, including Stream Decks, GamePads, and Makey Makey forwarding (which maps external inputs to arrow keys and other software triggers).

DMX

Adjust how lighting fixtures are handled in the user interface. You can choose to Show Master DMX Color, force MadMapper to Always draw fixtures pixels (even when unselected), and enable Automatically choose DMX address for duplicated / pasted fixture.

Audio

Manage your global audio routing.

  • Audio Settings: Select your specific Audio Input, Audio Analysis Channels, Audio Output, Sample Rate, and Buffer Size.

  • Audio Data: A read-only diagnostic window that provides a live status report of your active audio devices, channels, mixdown levels, and individual channel levels.

Engine

Manage backend rendering behaviors and preview quality.

  • Rendering: Displays your active GPU. You can toggle Use Double-Buffered Previews (which prevents screen tearing but impacts overall performance) and enable high-quality previews for Retina displays.

  • Media: Choose to enable audio playback by default, and define the default rendering resolution and frame rate for Image Folders.

Laser

See MadLaser Preferences for more details.

Enable global hardware protocols for your laser projectors.

  • Enable Audio Laser (AVB / Dante): Checking this box unlocks the ability to control laser projectors through audio output via an AVB or Dante network. Instead of using a standard ILDA DAC, MadMapper sends the X, Y, Red, Green, and Blue positional and color data directly to an AVB audio card as if it were an audio stream. This requires a compatible AVB network switch to guarantee bandwidth and an AVB audio interface (such as the RME Digiface AVB). Using AVB provides highly reliable signal transmission and allows for the perfect synchronization of multiple laser devices on the network.

  • Audio Device: Select your specific AVB or Dante network audio card. Note: On Windows, enabling AVB will force MadMapper to switch the audio driver type to ASIO and will require an application restart.

  • Sample Rate: Defines the transmission speed (e.g., 48000Hz or 96000Hz). You must ensure this exactly matches the sample rate set on your physical AVB / laser projector hardware.

  • Buffer Size: Set the network audio buffer (e.g., 192 samples).

  • Device Count: Allows you to choose the number of virtual AVB outputs you want to create, enabling you to drive multiple separate lasers from a single audio interface.

  • Audio Channels per Unit: Defines the number of audio channels dedicated to a single laser. This is typically set to 5 channels, representing the physical electrical signals required for X, Y, Red, Green, and Blue.

  • Enable Scene Markers: Toggle visibility for audio timeline markers.

  • Status Box: Provides a live diagnostic readout to confirm if the audio device is running properly and how many audio channels have been successfully started by the software.

Note: For a comprehensive guide on setting up your network switch, audio card, and hardware routing, the official MadLaser AVB Support guide can be found directly inside the software by navigating to the top menu and selecting Help > MadLaser User Guides > Mad Laser AVB Output.

Project Tab

These settings are saved directly into your current project workspace and will travel with the project if you move the project file to another computer.

Startup

Automate actions that should occur the moment this specific project is opened. Options include forcing the project into Fullscreen video mode upon opening, or automatically arming connected Laser projectors.

General

Manage project-level master recall behaviors.

  • Master: Choose whether to Restore Master Settings from Project when the file is loaded.

MIDI

Configure your project-specific MIDI routing and feedback.

  • MIDI Inputs: Select specific Input Devices and their corresponding Feedback Devices to keep MIDI controllers (like motorized faders or LED buttons) in sync with MadMapper. You can also choose to use note velocity when mapping.

  • MIDI Outputs: Define dedicated outgoing MIDI devices and names to trigger external hardware or software.

OSC

Manage incoming and outgoing Open Sound Control network data.

  • OSC Input: Set your listening Input Port (default 8010) and Feedback Port (default 9000). You can toggle Enable Bonjour Discovery for automatic network configuration and define a custom Feedback IP.

  • OSC Outputs: Create and manage a list of targeted outgoing OSC connections by defining their Name, IP, Port, and Bonjour status.

DMX

Configure incoming and outgoing lighting control data. MadMapper natively supports network protocols like Art-Net and sACN, as well as physical USB DMX interfaces (including the official MadMapper/GarageCube USB DMX controller, ShowJockey, Enttec DMX USB Pro, Enttec DMX USB Pro MK2, and any Enttec Pro compatible USB DMX device such as the DMX King eDMX2 Pro).

  • DMX Input: Define your listening device (e.g., ArtNet In), select the specific network interface, and set the listening universe.

  • DMX Output: Select your output protocol or physical device and target network interface. You can cap the Maximum FPS to optimize network traffic, enable Unicast routing, toggle Universe Synchronization, and utilize the built-in node scanner to auto-poll for active Art-Net devices on your network.

Engine

Project-specific rendering parameters for playback and media processing.

  • Rendering: Lock the Engine FPS to a specific frame rate or leave it on Auto to match your display.

  • Media: Globally toggle the Media Anti Aliasing filter for the project.

Timelines

Manage timeline playback conditions and legacy storage behaviors.

  • Playback & Storage: Options include automatically stopping active timelines when switching to a different Bank, and defining whether DMX Fixtures and Surface Output Geometries should be explicitly stored when recording legacy Scenes.

Laser

See MadLaser Preferences for more details.

This sub-menu contains critical safety and visualization settings for your project's laser outputs.

  • Security: Unlock Security Features to define the Max non-moving Beam Intensity (a critical safety parameter to prevent hardware damage or audience hazards) and enable Expert Mode Settings for advanced laser routing.

  • Visualisation: Route laser data over the network to supported external 3D visualizers like Capture.

  • Beam Preview: Adjust the internal rendering of the laser preview within the software UI. Options include setting the Beam Level (brightness), adjusting the Beam Origin X/Y coordinates to simulate the physical projector's location, toggling End Beam on path, and enabling a simulated Fog effect for accurate 3D previewing.

MadLaser Preferences

The foundational settings for laser output and safety are managed within the main MadMapper Preferences menu (Cmd + , on Mac / Ctrl + , on PC). Because lasers involve physical hardware and strict safety protocols, these settings are split between global application routing and project-specific safety limits.

Important Note: The settings detailed in the Laser tabs below are exclusive to the MadLaser extension. These menus and options will only appear in your preferences if the MadLaser extension is currently licensed and activated on your system.

⚠️ WARNING: LASER HAZARD Laser projectors can cause permanent harm if used incorrectly. Ensure your beam zones are safely clear of audiences and performers. It is your legal responsibility to understand and follow all laser safety regulations and reporting laws specific to your country before outputting high-power beams.

Application Tab > Laser

These settings govern global audio-to-laser network protocols on your specific computer, regardless of which project file is open.

  • Enable Audio Laser (AVB / Dante): Check this box to allow MadMapper to send laser control data over standard audio network protocols.

  • Audio Device & Channels: Select your target network audio interface (e.g., NDI Audio, Dante Virtual Soundcard) and configure the Sample Rate, Buffer Size, and Audio Channels per Unit.

  • Enable Scene Markers: Toggles the transmission of scene markers over the audio network.

 

Note: You must restart MadMapper for Audio Laser support to fully activate after changing these settings.

Project Tab > Laser

These settings contain critical safety and visualization parameters. Because they directly affect the physical output of the laser hardware, they are saved directly into your current .mad project file.

Security Settings 

By default, MadMapper limits certain laser parameters to protect both your audience and your hardware.

  • Unlock Security Features: Checking this box prompts a warning regarding the dangers of high-intensity beams. Unlocking this allows you to bypass the default safety constraints.

Max non-moving Beam Intensity: MadMapper natively prevents static (non-moving) beams from outputting at full power. This slider dictates the maximum brightness allowed when the scanners stop moving.

Safety Warning: A full-power, static beam from a professional laser can easily ignite fires or burn skin. Never increase this limit unless you are absolutely certain the beam path is safely terminated and clear of the audience.

Enable Expert Mode Settings

Enabling Expert Mode in your Project Preferences unlocks advanced, under-the-hood parameters within both the Laser Surface Inspector and Laser Output settings, designed specifically for complex installations and high-end hardware.

Hardware Warning: Scanning too fast can overheat and permanently damage the delicate galvo-scanners inside your laser projector. Only use Expert Mode if you know the exact physical limitations of your hardware.

Expert Mode unlocks the following Output-Level controls:

  • Custom PPS Range: Allows you to select "Custom" in your output device settings and manually define the scanning speed from 20 to 100,000 PPS. (Note: Pushing a low-end laser to 100kpps can permanently damage the hardware).

  • Expanded Blank Delay: Allows you to push the ILDA blanking delay down to 50% (normally restricted to a minimum of 100%). Lower values can cause drawing artifacts but are useful for highly specific hardware calibrations.

  • ILDA Mode (Preserve Image Quality vs. Preserve FPS): Unhides the ILDA Mode dropdown on your Laser Output.

    • Preserve Image Quality (Default): MadMapper prioritizes drawing every point accurately. If the composition is complex, the actual output frame rate may drop below your "Desired FPS".

    • Preserve FPS: MadMapper guarantees your target frame rate (e.g., locking to 60 FPS for video sync). To maintain this speed, the software will dynamically degrade image quality by removing angle points, or dropping paths entirely if the frame is too heavy.

Expert Mode Surface Features

  • RGB Samples (Laser Lines & Text): Increases the maximum allowable color sampling resolution up to 64k (default is 8k). Warning: 64k samples will have a heavy impact on software performance.

  • Expanded Speed Ranges: Increases the maximum allowed values for the Max Speed and Fixed Speed parameters up to 5.0 (normally restricted to 3.0 to protect entry-level scanners).

  • Start Repeat: Unhides a dedicated parameter allowing you to add extra dwell points specifically at the starting point of a path.

  • Advanced Video Vectorization: Unlocks deeper, experimental variables when converting standard video or images into laser paths (using "Find Paths" or "Find Contours").

  • Maximum Input Dimension: When vectorizing standard video files or images, MadMapper normally limits the maximum processed resolution to 8k to maintain real-time performance. Expert Mode unlocks a Maximum Input Dimension of 16k. While 16k video vectorization will likely cause real-time playback to stutter or drop frames, it is an incredibly powerful feature that allows you to use the Conductor Timeline to execute a non-real-time conversion of massive video files into high-resolution ILDA exports.

Visualisation & Beam Preview

These settings dictate how the laser output is simulated within MadMapper and sent to external pre-visualization software.

  • External Visualisation: Route the laser data to 3D simulation software (e.g., Capture, Depence 2, WYSIWYG).

  • Beam Preview: Adjust how the laser path is rendered on your computer screen.

    • Level: Adjusts the overall brightness of the preview.

    • Beam Origin: Click and drag the node on the X/Y grid to simulate the physical location of the laser projector relative to the output surface.

    • Enable Fog: Toggles a simulated atmospheric fog effect in the preview window to help visualize volumetric beams.

Project File Structure

Project Workspaces

MadMapper 6 introduces a major shift in how projects are saved and managed by moving from standalone project files to Project Workspaces.

Instead of generating a single .mad file that relies on external links to media scattered across your hard drive, MadMapper 6 now creates a dedicated, self-contained local workspace folder for your project with the extension .madproject.

The .madproject Workspace Folder

When you create and save a new project, MadMapper generates a master Workspace folder named [YourProjectName].madproject. By default, this directory is saved to Documents / MadMapper / [YourProjectName].madproject on your computer. Inside this folder, you will find:

  • The .mad Project Files: The core files containing your surfaces, routing, and show data (including your current working file and past saved versions).

  • Auto-Saves Folder: A dedicated subfolder containing your automated backups, keeping your main directory clean and uncluttered.

  • Resources Folder: Contains imported assets specific to the project, such as materials, generators, 3D objects, and other local data.

Collect External Resources

To fully consolidate your project, navigate to the File menu and select Collect External Resources....

When activated, MadMapper automatically gathers all external media you have referenced in your project (video files, audio tracks, images, textures, etc.) and copies them directly into your local .madproject Resources folder.

Workflow Benefits

Transitioning to this workspace structure drastically improves professional workflows:

  • Portability: By keeping everything contained within a single master .madproject folder, you can easily copy the workspace to an external drive. This allows you to open the project on another computer, or hand it off to a collaborator, without ever dealing with broken media links or "missing file" errors.

  • Organization: It acts as a proper production environment, keeping all assets, scripts, and backups strictly organized per project rather than globally scattered across your machine.

  • Archiving: When a live event or installation wraps, you can archive the single folder with 100% confidence that every component of the show is safely backed up together.

Merging Projects

The Merge Project... feature allows you to seamlessly import the contents of one MadMapper project directly into another.

This feature is incredibly useful for collaborative workflows, combining different elements of a show (like bringing a lighting designer's DMX fixture patch into a video operator's mapping file), or pulling a standardized template of surfaces into a brand-new venue setup without starting from scratch.

How to Merge Projects

To combine two projects, follow these steps:

  1. Open your Primary Project: Launch MadMapper and load the master .madproject workspace that you want to serve as the foundation of your show.

  2. Select Merge: Navigate to the top menu bar and select File > Merge Project...

  3. Choose the Source File: A file browser window will appear. Navigate to the secondary .mad file (or .madproject folder) that you wish to import and select it.

  4. Importing: MadMapper will process the selected file and append its contents directly into your current, active workspace.

What Gets Merged?

When you merge a project, MadMapper acts cumulatively, bringing in the elements of the secondary project without deleting or overwriting the existing data in your primary project. The merged components include:

  • Surfaces and Geometry: All video, light, and laser surfaces (Quads, Triangles, Lines, 3D Objects), retaining their input/output geometry, masks, and mesh warping.

  • Fixtures: All patched DMX fixtures, universes, and settings.

  • Media: Video files, images, generators, and materials loaded into the Media Bin.

  • Scenes and Cues: All programmed cues, scene states, and timeline data from the imported project.

  • Controls: Existing MIDI, OSC, and DMX mapping configurations linked to the imported setup.

Tip: After a successful merge, imported surfaces and fixtures will typically appear in their respective lists in the Tool Panels, and new media will be appended to your Media Bin. Organizing the imported items into dedicated Groups immediately after merging can help keep your interface clean.

Workspace Organization & Best Practices

Because MadMapper 6 utilizes a self-contained .madproject folder structure, merging a project from a different location on your hard drive means your primary project will now be temporarily referencing media files that live outside of its own workspace folder.

To maintain perfect project portability and organization, you should always consolidate your assets after a merge:

  1. Once your projects are merged, go to File > Collect External Resources...

  2. MadMapper will automatically locate all the newly imported media assets (videos, images, 3D files) and copy them directly into your primary .madproject Resources folder.

This guarantees that if you move your newly merged show file to a show computer or external drive, absolutely no media links will be broken.

Advanced MadMapper Configuration

 

The following pages are for advanced MadMapper power users who are looking to get the most out of the software.

Media Formats & Video Codecs

Selecting the appropriate video codec and media format is a critical factor for the performance and stability of MadMapper projects. Projection mapping frequently requires playing multiple high-resolution video streams simultaneously, which can heavily impact system resources if unoptimized formats are used.

While MadMapper utilizes native video engines and FFmpeg to leverage hardware decoding whenever possible, the formats you choose determine how efficiently your system can process the media.

Supported Media Formats

MadMapper utilizes FFmpeg and FreeImage backends, providing broad compatibility for a massive variety of video, image, and audio containers.

Supported Video Containers: mov, mpeg, mpg, mp4, m4v, mkv, avi, wmv, asf, gif, mts, ts, h264, flv, dnxhd, m2ts, vob, dv, webm

Supported Image Containers: jpg, jpeg, jp2, j2k, jxl, bmp, png, psd, exr, heic, hdr, raw, tiff, tif, sgi, ico, tga, dds, webp, pict, pdf, svg

Supported Audio Containers: wav, mp3, aac, flac, ogg, aif, aiff, m4a, ac3, wma

Supported Vector Animation: json (MadMapper supports Lottie format JSON files, allowing you to import vector animations directly from After Effects using the Bodymovin plugin).

(Note: NotchLC and DXV codecs are not currently supported).

 

Optimized Video Codecs for Live Performance

HAP Codec (Highly Recommended)

HAP is the industry-standard codec for live performance and multi-layer projection mapping.

  • How it works: HAP files are demuxed by FFmpeg, but MadMapper performs native HAP decoding directly on the GPU.

  • The Benefit: This enables the playback of multiple extremely high-resolution video layers with minimal risk of dropped frames. It is perfectly suited for rapid triggering, reverse playback, timeline scrubbing, and chunked decoding.

  • The Trade-off: HAP files require high disk read speeds and result in massive file sizes. Fast NVMe SSDs are required for multi-stream playback.

  • Variants: HAP (Standard), HAP Alpha (supports transparency), HAP Q (highest image quality). Note: HAP R is currently supported on Windows only.

More info at: https://hap.video/

Apple ProRes

ProRes is a high-quality alternative, exceptionally optimized for macOS.

  • The Benefit: It offers visually lossless quality with smaller file sizes than HAP. On macOS, MadMapper enables hardware acceleration for ProRes by default via Apple's VideoToolbox, providing vastly superior performance over standard CPU decoding.

  • The Trade-off: While highly efficient on Mac, ProRes generally requires more system resources than HAP when playing a high number of simultaneous layers, and is not recommended for Windows playback.

H.264, HEVC (H.265), AV1, and H.266

While MadMapper fully supports modern delivery codecs like H.264, HEVC, AV1, and H.266 (via FFmpeg), they require careful consideration when used for live projection mapping.

  • The Challenge: These are highly compressed "inter-frame" codecs designed primarily to save file size rather than optimize real-time playback.

  • The Result: They require significant CPU processing power to decode. Playing multiple heavily compressed clips simultaneously, reversing playback, or scrubbing the timeline may lead to dropped frames or stuttering. (Note: If forced to choose for file-size reasons, H.264 decodes faster than HEVC).

  • The Workaround: If you are using H.264 for non-linear playback, rapid triggering, or timeline scratching, configure your video export settings to generate a keyframe for every single frame (often called an "All-Intra" setting or a Keyframe Distance of 1). This increases the file size but removes the heavy mathematical decoding calculations, significantly reducing CPU bottlenecks.

Hardware Decoding vs. FFmpeg Processing

MadMapper handles hardware decoding differently depending on your operating system to ensure stability. If hardware acceleration fails or is unsupported for a specific file, MadMapper will seamlessly fall back to the FFmpeg CPU decoder.

macOS Decoding

  • ProRes: Hardware acceleration is enabled by default (via VideoToolbox) and is highly optimal.

  • H.264 / HEVC Limitations: While users can enable hardware acceleration for these formats via Apple's AVFoundation framework, there is a known OS-level limitation regarding audio routing. AVFoundation forces audio to route to the macOS system default output, bypassing MadMapper's internal audio preferences. Because of this, it is generally recommended to leave hardware acceleration off for these formats and rely on MadMapper's highly optimized FFmpeg implementation to ensure proper audio routing.

Windows (PC) Decoding

  • DXVA 2: On Windows, Hardware Acceleration is disabled by default. This is because non-Direct3D implementations require a GPU-to-CPU-to-GPU "ping-pong" data transfer that mitigates performance gains, and hardware drivers can occasionally be unstable with specific codecs.

  • Enabling: You can manually enable Windows hardware decoding via DXVA 2 by going to Project Preferences > Engine > Media and checking "Enable Hardware Acceleration Option".

Image Sequences (Folder Player)

For pristine, uncompressed playback, MadMapper allows you to load entire folders of images and play them back as a video sequence.

  • Naming Convention: To ensure proper playback order, files must be named sequentially with padded zeros (e.g., 00001_image.png, 00002_image.png, 00003_image.png).

  • Limits: There is no maximum limit to the number of images in a folder sequence (1,000,000+ files will load seamlessly).

  • Playback Controls: Image sequences feature the exact same playback modes as standard movies, allowing you to loop, ping-pong, hold, and scrub the sequence.

Advanced Image Formats

EXR (32-bit Floating Point)

MadMapper fully supports high-dynamic-range EXR image files. The software utilizes the FreeImage library to parse the EXR and converts the data directly into a 32-bit floating-point format for internal rendering. This massive dynamic range and precision makes EXR files exceptionally useful for driving custom shaders, creating high-end displacement maps, or precisely controlling laser variables.

Supported Channels & Conversion: Depending on your export settings from other software, MadMapper processes EXR files into the following formats:

  • Single Channel (Red): If the EXR is exported as a 64-bit IEEE floating point (FIT_DOUBLE), MadMapper will convert and optimize it into a 1-channel, 32-bit float Red image.

  • Multi-Channel (RGBA): If the EXR is exported as a 96-bit RGB float (FIT_RGBF) or 128-bit RGBA float (FIT_RGBAF), MadMapper will convert it directly into a standard 4-channel RGBA 32-bit float image.

SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics)

MadMapper supports direct SVG imports.

  • For Video Surfaces: You can manually define the exact pixel resolution you wish the SVG to render at, allowing for infinite scaling without rasterized pixelation.

  • For Laser Surfaces: Render size parameters are ignored, as the laser engine directly traces the mathematically pure vector paths of the SVG for its scanner output.

Quick Usage Example

A simple Material using all three libraries:

 
/*{
    "CREDIT": "Your Name",
    "DESCRIPTION": "Noisy glowing circle",
    "INPUTS": [
        {"LABEL": "Radius", "NAME": "mat_radius", "TYPE": "float", "DEFAULT": 0.25, "MIN": 0.0, "MAX": 0.5}
    ]
}*/

#include "MadCommon.glsl"
#include "MadNoise.glsl"
#include "MadSDF.glsl"

vec4 materialColorForPixel(vec2 texCoord)
{
    vec2 uv = texCoord - vec2(0.5);

    // Distort the domain with noise
    float n = noise(uv * 10.0 + TIME) * 0.02;

    // Create a circle using SDF
    float sdf = circle(uv + n, mat_radius);

    // Color it using MadCommon's hsv2rgb
    vec3 col = hsv2rgb(vec3(TIME * 0.1, 0.8, 1.0));

    vec3 color = vec3(0.0);
    color = fill(color, col, sdf);
    color += glow(col * 0.5, sdf, 0.1);

    return vec4(color, 1.0);
}

DMX Fixture Definitions

Overview

A DMX Fixture Definition describes the channel layout of a DMX lighting device so MadMapper knows how to control it. MadMapper ships with a built-in library of common fixtures (generic RGB pixels, RGBW strips, etc.), but you can create custom definitions for any DMX device — moving heads, laser fixtures, LED bars, fog machines, or complex multi-channel fixtures like the Minuit Une IVL Dice.

Fixture definitions are stored as .mmfl files (MadMapper Fixture Library). These files can be imported, exported, and shared between projects and users.

 

Fixture Editor

Opening the Editor

  1. Go to the DMX Fixtures tab (Cmd+4 / Ctrl+4)
  2. Click DMX + to create a new fixture
  3. In the fixture's properties, click Edit next to Fixture Library

This opens the Fixture Editor panel, which lists all available fixture definitions — both built-in and custom.

Keyboard shortcut to open the Fixture Editor panel directly: Option+Cmd+F (Mac) / Alt+Ctrl+F (Windows)

Creating a New Fixture

  1. In the Fixture Editor, click the + button
  2. Set the fixture name and group (used for organization in the library)
  3. Define the pixel grid dimensions (Width × Height) — use 1×1 for non-pixel fixtures
  4. Set the Pixel Type to Custom for non-standard channel layouts
  5. Add channels in order, specifying each channel's type, label, and bit depth

Fixture Properties

When creating or editing a fixture in the Fixture Editor, the Properties panel provides the following options:

 

Size Mode

Option Description
Fixed Size Manually set the pixel grid dimensions (Width × Height)
LED Strip Mode Configure as a linear strip of pixels
Matrix Mode Configure as a 2D pixel grid

Pixel Type — Select the color model for the fixture's pixels: RGB, RGBW, or Custom (for non-standard channel layouts like the IVL Dice).

Pixel Size — The number of DMX channels per pixel (e.g., 3 for RGB, 4 for RGBW). Check Advanced to access per-channel type and label configuration.

Assignation — Defines the pixel scanning/addressing order for LED strips and matrices. The 16 arrow pattern icons represent different ways pixels can be wired through the grid: left-to-right then top-to-bottom (Z-pattern), serpentine/zigzag, bottom-to-top, column-first, and their mirrored and reversed variants. Select the pattern that matches how your LEDs are physically wired. Click Clear to reset.

Skip channels 511–512 — When enabled, MadMapper will leave DMX channels 511 and 512 empty at the end of each universe. Some DMX devices reserve these channels, and enabling this avoids addressing conflicts at universe boundaries.

Channel Types

Each channel in a fixture definition has a type that tells MadMapper how to interpret it:

Type Description Typical Use
R Red RGB/RGBW color mixing
G Green RGB/RGBW color mixing
B Blue RGB/RGBW color mixing
W White RGBW fixtures
L Luminance Single-channel brightness
C Cyan CMY color mixing
M Magenta CMY color mixing
Y Yellow CMY color mixing
Slider Generic DMX value (0–255) Dimmer, pan, tilt, speed, gobo, or any non-color channel with manual control
Expression GLSL expression Computed channel value driven by a formula (see Expression Channels below)
Unused Empty/skipped channel Placeholder for reserved or unneeded channels in the fixture's DMX footprint

Bit Depth

Channels can be set to 8 Bits (single channel, 0–255) or 16 Bits (two channels, coarse + fine, 0–65535). For 16-bit control using 8-bit channels, create two consecutive entries — a coarse and a fine — as seen in the IVL Dice example (e.g., "Index" and "Index Fine"). Alternatively, set a single channel to 16 Bits and MadMapper will handle both DMX channels automatically.

Expression Channels

Expression channels let you compute a DMX value using a GLSL expression instead of a fixed slider or color input. This is useful for deriving channel values from other parameters — for example, calculating a checksum, inverting a value, or mixing multiple inputs mathematically.

 

The following variables are available inside an expression:

Variable Description
R, G, B Current red, green, and blue color values
L Luminance value
W White value
C, M, Y Cyan, magenta, and yellow values
INDEX The pixel index within the fixture
posX, posY Normalized pixel position within the fixture grid
COMP Component index
time Current time value
Slider names The values of any Slider channels, referenced by their label name

Expressions follow GLSL syntax, so standard math functions like sin(), clamp(), mix(), step(), etc. are available.

Real-World Example: Minuit Une IVL Dice (Mode 1, 33 Channels)

For standard pixel mapping with addressable RGBW LED pixels, a fixture will not require this comprehensive of a definition. But this example shows how MadMapper fixtures can be customized to work with any DMX protocol device — a two-channel hazer that uses sliders to regulate haze and fan speeds, a DMX drop system, a moving head, or in this case, a laser fixture with dozens of parameters.

This fixture has four independent laser emitters, each with tilt, dimmer, and RGB control, plus global parameters for shutter, beam count, rotation, and beam size. It uses a 1×1 pixel grid with type Custom because it is not a pixel-mapped device — each channel serves a specific mechanical or optical function. The RGB values have been assigned to the corresponding color channels from the manufacturer's channel layout.

 

 

 

Importing and Exporting

Import a Fixture Definition

  1. Open the Fixture Editor (click Edit next to Fixture Library on any fixture, or use Option+Cmd+F / Alt+Ctrl+F)
  2. Click Import...
  3. Select a .mmfl file
  4. The fixture appears in the library and is ready to assign

Export a Fixture Definition

  1. Open the Fixture Editor
  2. Select the fixture you want to export
  3. Click Export...
  4. Save the .mmfl file to share or back up

Exported .mmfl files can be shared with other MadMapper users, committed to a Git repository, or included with a project archive.

Import Fixtures from CSV

For large installations with many fixtures, MadMapper supports CSV import to batch-create fixtures with names, groups, and DMX addresses. Since MadMapper 5.2, the CSV can include group hierarchy using / notation (e.g., "Stage Fixtures/Fixture 1"). See File > Import DMX Fixtures from CSV for details.

Import Fixtures from SVG

For spatial layouts, MadMapper can import fixture positions from SVG files created in Illustrator or similar tools. This is especially useful for complex LED installations where fixture placement and DMX patching need to match a physical design precisely.

Tips for Custom Fixtures

Naming conventions — Use clear, descriptive channel labels. Include "Fine" in the label for the LSB channel of 16-bit pairs so operators can quickly identify coarse/fine relationships.

Modes — Many fixtures have multiple DMX modes with different channel counts. Create a separate definition for each mode and include the mode in the product name (e.g., "Minuit Une IVL Dice Mode 1").

Testing — After creating a fixture definition, use the DMX Monitor panel (Option+Cmd+M / Alt+Ctrl+M) to verify that channels are mapping correctly and values are reaching the expected DMX addresses.

Color channel types — Use the correct R/G/B/W/C/M/Y types for color channels rather than Slider. This allows MadMapper's color engine to properly drive them with pixel-mapped media, materials, and color pickers.

Cross-universe fixtures — If your fixture spans more than 512 channels or if its DMX address places it near the end of a universe, enable avoidCrossUniversePixels to prevent a single pixel's channels from being split across two universes.

Backup — Keep your custom .mmfl files in a shared location or version control. Fixture definitions are stored within MadMapper's library, but having external backups ensures you can quickly rebuild on a new machine.
