Mad AI Extension

Mad AI is an integrated, AI-powered content generation tool that allows you to create custom, real-time generative materials (GLSL shaders) purely through text prompts, with no coding knowledge required.

  • Accessing Mad AI: Navigate to the AI / Code Editor, click the + (Plus) button to create a new material. Check the box for "Using MadAI" to open the AI prompt interface.

  • Parametric Controls: Mad AI does not just generate a static video; it generates dynamic math. The AI automatically builds custom user interface sliders for the parameters you request.

  • Code Integration: At any time, you can toggle from the AI interface directly to the raw Code Editor. This is an excellent way to learn GLSL coding or manually tweak the math generated by the AI.

  • Credit System: Processing is handled securely via MadMapper's servers. Every prompt sent to the server consumes one credit from your MadMapper user account.

 

To purchase more MadAI credits, go here: http://madmapper.com/extensions/madai

Prompting Best Practices & Cheat Sheet

To get the best results from Mad AI, you should make short iterative prompts as opposed to one big descriptive prompt. For example:

  1. First, prompt the system to create a sphere in 3d with lighting.

  2. Second, add a prompt to add camera angle controls.

  3. Finally, add a prompt to add depth fog.

When building your prompts, utilizing specific terminology yields the best generative results. Use the following vocabulary reference:

  • Basic Shapes: sphere, cube, pyramid, platonic solid, torus, capsule, cylinder, plane.

  • Rendering Styles: 3d, raymarching, sdf, ambient occlusion, lighting, shading.

  • Lighting & Details (Specular): diffuse lighting, soft shadow, hard shadow, fresnel, bloom, glow, outline, curvature, normal displacement, deformation, greeble, repeat in X Y Z axis, pMod, depth fog.

  • Noises: fBm, vnoise, voronoi, flowNoise.

  • Camera Controls: camera angle, camera orbit, FOV.

  • Animation Behaviors: breathe, wobble, flicker, bounce, rotozoom, sine warp.

 

When you material is ready, you can rename it, tweak it, and share it with the world.  See the Online Material Library documentation for more information.

MadProjectorControl

The MadProjectorControl extension (listed under the Modules) allows you to control your video-projectors remotely through the network using the PJLink protocol. You can remotely power your PJLink-enabled projectors on and off, as well as mute their video and audio signal at will. With the help of MadMapper's Calendar Scheduler & Cue Scheduler, you can fully automate your installation, removing the need for a dedicated operator.

 

Installation & Setup

  • Authorisation: Within MadMapper, click on the Account menu in the top bar, then select Manage Authorisations. Select MadProjector Control and follow the procedure. The admin password of your computer will be asked before restarting.

  • Adding the Module: Go to the Modules tab accessible from the top left of the interface. Click on the icon at the left of the Modules list to add a module and select PJLink. You must add a PJLink module instance for each projector you want to control.

  • Network Prerequisites: For power saving reasons, the projector's network interface may be disabled when the projector is turned off. You may want to disable this power saving feature if MadMapper is supposed to turn on the projector. Once the green LED on the projector's Ethernet connector is lit, you can test connectivity by pinging the projector on the network.

Target Configuration

Once connected to the same ethernet network, you must setup the Target fields of the module first.

  • Device Selection: Relying on the PJLink discovery protocol, all supported-devices IP addresses will appear in the Device dropdown list, which can take up to 30 seconds after MadMapper has started.

  • Manual Setup: Since the protocol is not supported by all PJLink-enabled devices, you can otherwise manually input the projector IP by selecting Custom Device.

  • Security: Depending on the projector's model and configuration, you may need to enter a password to connect to the device.

Controls & Info

Once the status becomes connected, you will get access to the Power and Mute Controls.

  • Power Behavior: When changed, the Power button represents the desired power state of the projector. The desired state may not be reached immediately; for example, if the projector is still cooling down, the order will be delayed until it is enabled to be powered on again.

  • Mute Behavior: Click the Mute button to mute or unmute both the audio and video of the projector. Video mute can have different effects depending on the projector's technology, such as engaging a motorized physical shutter on older models, or instantly cutting the light-source on newer models. The projector's Mute status will remain blank until the device gets powered on.

  • Bidirectional Feedback: In the absence of control changes in the module, the Power and Mute button states will match the actual state of the projector. If the projector gets powered off or muted using the device's physical remote, the PJLink module will eventually update to reflect the new state.

  • Projector Info: The Info section will display the projector's Name, Model, Brand, Serial, and Format once the Status becomes connected. The projector's Format will remain blank until the projector is turned on and receives a signal.

Performance Optimization (Large Installations)

When pushing millions of pixels to multiple outputs, balancing your CPU, GPU, and internal storage bandwidth is critical.

GPU Tuning & The Frame Tearing Problem

  • macOS: Modern Apple Silicon (M-Series) machines utilize unified memory, making them exceptionally efficient for large-scale video processing, especially when utilizing native ProRes hardware acceleration to bypass CPU bottlenecks.

  • Windows (PC): A dedicated, high-end NVIDIA GPU is heavily recommended. However, simply plugging four projectors into the four ports of a standard consumer NVIDIA RTX card will almost always result in frame tearing. Because consumer cards cannot perfectly synchronize the refresh cycles of multiple independent display heads, fast-moving horizontal visuals will look fractured across your projectors.

  • The Media Server Solution: To achieve true, genlocked frame synchronization across multiple GPU outputs on a PC, you must use a professional-grade NVIDIA Quadro card paired with a dedicated Quadro Sync II card to lock the outputs to a master timing signal.

The Hardware Splitter Strategy

To guarantee perfect frame sync without building a highly complex Quadro Sync media server, the industry-standard approach is to utilize external display controllers.

  • How it Works: You drive a single, massive 4K or 8K output from your computer's GPU. Because the computer only sees one physical display, frame tearing is impossible. That single high-resolution signal is then routed into a hardware splitter, which physically divides the raster into multiple independent 1080p or 4K feeds for your projectors.

  • Industry Standards: Devices like the Datapath Fx4 (or Fx4-HDR) can take a single 4K60 signal over DisplayPort and flawlessly slice it into four synchronized HD outputs. Other reliable alternatives include the Matrox QuadHead2Go, or utilizing PCIe capture/playback cards like the Blackmagic DeckLink 8K Pro configured for quad-split output.

Storage Bandwidth & The HAP Codec

For large installations, relying on highly compressed delivery formats (like H.264 or HEVC) will instantly bottleneck your CPU as it struggles to decode the math in real-time, resulting in stuttering playback.

  • The HAP Strategy: You must render your installation media using the HAP codec family (HAP for standard playback, HAP Alpha for transparency, or HAP Q for higher visual fidelity). HAP bypasses the CPU entirely and sends the video decompression workload straight to the GPU.

  • The NVMe Bottleneck: The trade-off for zero CPU load is massive file sizes. Standard 5400RPM or 7200RPM spinning hard drives cannot read data fast enough to play multiple HAP files. You must use high-speed internal PCIe NVMe M.2 SSDs (capable of 3,000 to 7,000 MB/s read speeds) or high-bandwidth Thunderbolt RAID arrays.

  • Benchmarking: Always benchmark your storage drives using tools like the Blackmagic Disk Speed Test. You must mathematically ensure that the sustained read speed of your drive heavily exceeds the combined total megabytes-per-second of all the video files playing in your timeline simultaneously.

Network Bandwidth & NDI Stream Management

If you are routing live generative video between computers (e.g., from a dedicated TouchDesigner PC into a MadMapper Mac) using NDI, you must carefully manage your network topology.

  • Bandwidth Math: A single 1080p 60fps NDI High Bandwidth stream consumes roughly 125 to 150 Mbps of network data.

  • Gigabit Limitations: Sending multiple uncompressed NDI streams will quickly saturate a standard 1-Gigabit (1,000 Mbps) network switch. Network engineers strongly recommend leaving 25% to 30% of your network as "headroom" to prevent packet loss. If your NDI traffic exceeds 750 Mbps, your streams will begin to stutter and drop frames.

  • 10GbE Infrastructure: For large-scale installations requiring multiple 4K NDI feeds, upgrading your infrastructure to a 10-Gigabit (10GbE) managed network switch and utilizing Cat6a ethernet cabling is strictly required to ensure stable, zero-latency transmission.

Project Backup & Recovery

MadMapper features robust integrated tools to protect complex mapping data, hardware routing, and generative programming from accidental loss.  Outside of your standard, File > Save Project or Save Project As, MadMapper offers additional options to configure your setup to keep your projects safe as you continue to work on them.

AutoSave System

MadMapper operates a background AutoSave mechanism that routinely creates recovery snapshots of your workspace. Because AutoSave does not overwrite your actual project file, you can always reload the project to the exact state you manually saved it.

  • Configuration: You can enable this feature and set the save interval (e.g., every 5 minutes) by navigating to Preferences > General.

  • File Location: When AutoSave is on and the project is modified, the current state is saved to an autosave file located in the MadMapperProjectData/ sub-folder.

  • The 10-Second Countdown: A countdown will appear 10 seconds before the AutoSave triggers. This gives you time to disable it in case you are live and want to preserve your project's saved state, or if you simply don't want the background save process to cause a dip in the application framerate.

  • Toolbar Control: When enabled in Preferences, the feature is active by default, but you can temporarily deactivate it until the application quits by clicking the AutoSave button in the toolbar. (If AutoSave is completely disabled in Preferences, this toolbar button will be greyed out).

  • Crash Recovery: If your computer or the application unexpectedly quits, the next time you launch it, MadMapper will propose you to recover the AutoSave state.

Project Backup

In addition to the automated background snapshots, MadMapper maintains a localized history of your manual saves.

  • Version History: When saving a project, MadMapper will automatically backup the previous version in the MadMapperProjectData/ sub-folder.

  • Max Backup Count: Located in Preferences > General right beneath the AutoSave settings, this setting controls the maximum number of backups stored for the current project.

Workspaces & File Collect

Large projection mapping projects often rely on hundreds of scattered media files, custom shaders, and 3D models. You can define a specific global folder as your Workspace. When archiving or moving to a show computer, use the File Collect feature to automatically gather and package every piece of media referenced in your project into one consolidated directory. This prevents "Missing File" errors and makes it easy to back up the entire installation to an external drive or cloud-sync service.

 

 

Export Project To

File > Export Project To is a way to export your complete MadMapper project folder with all resources (option) to a new destination.  If you are passing your project off to a client or exporting to an external hard drive, this method will make sure that all the necessary information is saved to your new destination.

Arduino & Firmata Integration

MadMapper supports direct, bidirectional communication with physical microcontrollers using the Firmata protocol. This allows you to easily route physical sensors, buttons, and potentiometers directly into MadMapper as control inputs, or send data out from MadMapper to trigger physical hardware like LEDs, motors, and relays.

 

Arduino Software & Guides

  • Arduino IDE Download: https://www.arduino.cc/en/software

  • Arduino Official Documentation & Tutorials: https://docs.arduino.cc/

Firmata Protocol

  • Firmata Official Website: https://firmata.org/

  • Firmata Protocol Documentation (GitHub): https://github.com/firmata/protocol

  • Arduino Firmata Library Repository: https://github.com/firmata/arduino

Supported Boards & Hardware

  • Universal Compatibility: While the MadMapper interface explicitly highlights popular boards such as the Arduino Uno, Arduino Mega, and Teensy, the software does not check VendorID or ProductID. Therefore, any connected microcontroller that registers as a valid serial port on your computer will appear as an option.

  • The Rule of Thumb: If you can successfully upload the Standard Firmata sketch to your board via the Arduino IDE, you can use it to communicate with MadMapper.

Preparing the Microcontroller (Arduino IDE 2.x)

Before MadMapper can see your board, you must install the Firmata library onto it.

  1. Download and open the latest version of the official Arduino IDE (Version 2.x or newer).

  2. Connect your Arduino or microcontroller to your computer via USB.

  3. In the new Arduino IDE, look at the top toolbar. Click the Board Selection Dropdown and select your connected board and its corresponding serial port. (Note: Many official Arduino boards will be automatically detected and selected here).

  4. Navigate to the top menu and click File > Examples > Firmata > StandardFirmata.

    • (Note: If you are using an Arduino Mega or a Teensy, you must select StandardFirmataPlus instead).

  5. Click the Upload button (the right-pointing arrow in the top-left corner of the toolbar).

  6. Wait for the terminal at the bottom of the screen to display the "Done uploading" message. Once successful, close the Arduino IDE completely.

Connecting to MadMapper

Once the board is flashed with Firmata, you can connect it to your MadMapper project:

  1. Open the Modules tab (accessible from the top left of the main interface).

  2. Click the + (Plus) icon to add a new module and select Firmata.

  3. In the Firmata module's Configuration settings, use the Port dropdown to select your board's serial connection (e.g., /dev/cu.usbmodem... on Mac or COM3 on Windows).

  4. Select your exact Model (e.g., Arduino UNO) from the dropdown.

Working with Pins and Modes

Once connected, the module will display a list of all available Analog and Digital pins on your board. You can configure each pin's Mode based on what physical component is wired to it:

  • Analog Mode: Use this for variable physical sensors, such as photo-resistors or knobs. Any changes in voltage will instantly reflect in MadMapper as a continuous value.

  • Input Mode: Use this for simple digital switches and buttons (e.g., pressed vs. unpressed).

  • Output Mode: Use this to send a basic On/Off signal from MadMapper to trigger external hardware (like a relay or a simple LED).

  • PWM Mode (Pulse Width Modulation): Use this to send variable data out of MadMapper, such as smoothly dimming an LED's brightness intensity using a slider. (Note: On the Arduino UNO specifically, you cannot properly use PWM and Servo modes simultaneously due to hardware timer limitations).

  • Servo Mode: Use this to convert data from MadMapper into physical movement, driving the angle of a connected servo motor.

Mapping Firmata Controls

You can map any parameter in MadMapper directly to your physical Arduino sensors or actuators using the Control List.

  1. Right-click the parameter you want to link in MadMapper, and select Add Control > MadMapper > Firmata.

  2. Set the Source Device to Firmata.

  3. Select the specific Channel that corresponds to your pin (e.g., D7 State for a digital button, or A0 for an analog photo-resistor).

  4. Use the Source Range and Target Range sliders to scale the behavior. For example, you can map the true/false state of a physical button press to drive a value from 0 to 255, which could trigger an LED or rotate a servo motor exactly 180 degrees.

Timelines

Timelines Overview & The Conductor

MadMapper 6 introduces a monumental shift in how you program and execute shows: the native Timeline system. Previously, complex projects relied entirely on state-based logic, where you triggered isolated snapshots and let the software crossfade between them. With the introduction of Timelines, MadMapper steps into the role of a centralized, non-linear show control system.

The Conductor acts as your Master Timeline. This is where you can build out a linear sequence that controls almost all aspects of your project simultaneously. Within the Conductor, you can create interactive flags (Markers) to pause, loop, or jump through the sequence. You can drop entire Scenes and Cues directly into a Timeline Player track, while simultaneously controlling non-linear montage tracks, routing video and audio sources, driving geometric surfaces, firing lasers, running DMX lighting sequences, and outputting MIDI/OSC commands to external systems.

Use the shortcut Cmd + Shift + C (Mac) or Ctrl + Shift + C (Windows) to instantly access Edit Mode for The Scenes and Cues.

Scenes & Cues

Before diving into timeline animation, it is important to understand MadMapper's foundational state-recall system.

  • Scenes (Global Snapshots): A Scene acts as an absolute master snapshot of your entire project, recording the exact state of every surface, fixture, and media file.

  • Cues (Granular States): Cues offer surgical precision, allowing you to store and recall only a specific selection of parameters (e.g., just the geometry of one quad) without affecting the rest of your live output.

  • Quick Fade Transitions: Underneath the name of each Scene and Cue in the grid, you can double-click on the time (default 0s) to quickly change the fade transition duration.

Operator Note: While Scenes are great, Cues are extremely powerful. They allow you to make dynamic changes to a live show or project, while keeping your main media playing continuously. While it is possible to modify a Scene to keep playing media when triggered, by default, a scene will store all aspects of your project, which can lead to media restarting, or unexpected behavior while fading between Scenes. Get to know Cues and they'll be a great tool.

Editing & Updating Scenes and Cues

 

If you tweak a Scene or Cue during a show, your live changes are not saved automatically. When editing parameters, keep an eye on the interface highlights: Red highlights indicate that a parameter is currently editable, and a red line means it has been edited. Orange indicates that a parameter is currently selected (or, in batch updating, that the current values differ from the other selected Scenes and Cues).

MadMapper provides three distinct workflows to save your adjustments:

  • The Record Button: Select the Scene or Cue, click the Record button, and edit your values as desired. Click the Record button again to stop editing and save your changes.

    • Batch Updating: If you want to update values across multiple scenes simultaneously, select all the desired scenes, click Record, make your changes, and click Record again to save those new values to every selected item.

  • The Right-Click Method: Make your live adjustments, then right-click the specific Scene or Cue in the grid and select Update Scene (or Update Cue) to overwrite it with your current output.

  • Drag & Drop (Cues Only): For a fast, modular workflow with Cues, simply make your adjustments and drag the modified Media or Surface directly on top of the existing Cue to overwrite it (or drop it into an empty slot to create a brand new one).

Right-Click Scene & Cue Options

Right-clicking directly on a Scene or Cue in the grid opens a context menu with several management options.

  • Update / Update Startup Values: Instantly overwrites the saved state with your current live output parameters.

  • Add To Timeline: Pushes the state directly into the Conductor. For Cues, you can choose to send all objects, or filter the push to only include specific elements like Video Surfaces, Lasers, Fixtures, or Medias.

  • Layout: Allows you to insert or delete rows and columns to organize your grid.

  • Add Control / Copy OSC Address: Quickly maps external triggers to fire the Scene/Cue.

Pro-Tip: Saving Your Changes If you make live adjustments to a Scene, remember to right-click it and select Update Scene to save your work.

You can do the exact same thing for Cues, but Cues also offer a faster workflow: simply make your adjustments and drag the modified Media or Surface directly over the existing Cue to overwrite it, or drop it into an empty slot to create a brand new one.

Scene & Cue Settings (Three Dots Menu)

 

Clicking the three dots on a Scene or Cue opens its dedicated settings panel to define how it fires and looks in your grid.

  • Launch & Transition: Define the Launch Quantize behavior to lock triggers to the beat, select the Transition Type (e.g., Linear), and set the fade Duration in seconds.

  • Representation: Customize the button's appearance in the grid by assigning a specific color code, uploading a custom image (or using the media thumbnail), and writing a text Comment for your operator.

Turning Cues into Timelines

With MadMapper 6, Scenes and Cues are no longer just static snapshots; they can become distinct Timelines themselves. This allows you to fine-tune transitions, precisely modify parameter changes down to the millisecond, and animate elements for live busking or pre-planned shows.

 

Accessing Edit Mode & Animating

To begin modifying or animating a cue, you must first enter Edit Mode. You can do this in two ways:

  1. Right-Click: Right-click an existing Scene or Cue in the grid and select Edit.

  2. The Edit Button: Alternatively, you can click the Edit button located at the bottom right of the main Scenes & Cues UI.

 

Once in Edit mode, the Scenes and Cues timeline will appear at the bottom of your screen, presenting the option to animate your parameters.

 

 

Clicking the Animate button instantly creates a timeline track within that specific cue where you can begin adding keyframes or recording new elements.

 

After clicking Animate, you will be given a timeline track for the specific scene or cue that you have selected. From here you can animate your sequences using the same timeline editing logic (see below).

 

The Scenes & Cues Inspector

To view and modify the deep settings of your cues and tracks, you need to utilize the Inspector panel.

  • Toggling the Inspector: When you select a track value or cue, you can toggle the inspector panel open using the Inspector button on the far right of the interface. 

(Note: You will simply see "No Selection" displayed in the panel if a track or cue is not actively selected). 

When you select an active Scene or Cue, the Inspector reveals how it interacts with the timeline:

  • Update from current values: A prominent button to quickly overwrite the stored state with your current live output.

  • Track Transition: When this cue is dropped into a master timeline, you can define how this clip transitions. You can choose No transition, Use timeline transition settings (inheriting global rules), or Use local transition settings (allowing you to set a custom duration in seconds just for this instance).

Timeline Navigation & UI Controls

Navigating complex timelines requires efficient zooming and track management. MadMapper provides several shortcuts and UI toggles to speed up your workflow:

  • Horizontal Zoom: Hold Option + Scroll Up/Down to shrink or expand the timeline horizontally.

  • Vertical Track Zoom: Hold Command + Scroll Up/Down to expand or collapse the tracks vertically.

  • Clip Navigation: Press Tab to jump the playhead to the next clip on the track. Press Shift + Tab to move to the previous clip.

Filters:

  • Track Pinning: Click the Pin icon to isolate and show only the tracks you have actively pinned. Pinned tracks will also show their respective keyframes.

  • Show Animated Tracks: Click the stopwatch icon to filter the view, showing only tracks that contain active keyframes.

  • Search: Use the search bar to instantly locate a specific element or parameter track by name.

Timeline Settings & Time Formatting

 

 

You can customize how time is calculated and displayed across your sequence. By clicking the Three Dots (...) icon in the upper timeline toolbar, you can access the core settings:

  • FPS → BPM Setup: Define the relationship between your frame rate and musical tempo by setting your target FPS, master BPM, and musical Signature (e.g., 4/4 time).

  • Playback Mode: Choose how the timeline advances. Options include Default (internal clock), Controlled Speed (variable playback rate), Global BPM (locked to the main MadMapper tempo), or External Sync (driven by incoming timecode).

  • Ruler Formatting: Change the visual increments on your timeline ruler by selecting the dropdown next to the time display. View your timeline in Seconds, exact Frames, or musical beat divisions ranging from 1/32 notes up to 4 bars (or turn it Off).

Timeline Right-Click Operations

 

Right-clicking directly on the timeline ruler or an empty track space provides high-level arrangement tools:

  • Display: A quick toggle to switch the ruler formatting between Time, Time/Frames, or Time/Bars.

  • Add Keyframes: Instantly drop keyframes across all tracks or only modified tracks at the playhead.

  • Insert / Delete Time: Opens a dialog to shift the entire arrangement forward or backward by a specific duration.

  • Loop Controls: Rapidly define the active loop bracket by selecting Set as Loop Start, Set as Loop End, or Move Loop here.

Creating & Editing Timelines (Keyframes)

A Scene or Cue that is converted into a timeline will include the track parameters within MadMapper that it has saved. So for example, if your Scene or Cue is assigned to a specific surface, FX, or UI element (Sliders, Buttons, Sources, etc.) then those stored settings will appear in the list of tracks.

 

 

To modify keyframes, add new tracks to the timeline, or add new parameters, simply click the Record button at the top of the timeline you are trying to edit. Then click on the UI element or slider that you'd like to change, and MadMapper will automatically create a keyframe for that element based on the values you've selected.  With Record button still active you can advance through the timeline and make new adjustments, and add new tracks and keyframes to your existing timeline.  When you are done, simply click the Record button again to disable it.

When a track has been created, you can double-click with your mouse on the keyframe line and it will create a new keyframe that you can modify further.

 

When a parameter track is armed, any changes you make in the interface will generate a keyframe. Right-clicking on any recorded keyframe opens the interpolation menu, allowing you to define the mathematical transition between points:

  • None (n): The value holds flat and instantly snaps to the next keyframe.

  • Linear (l): Creates a constant, straight-line transition between two values.

  • Bezier (b): Adds adjustable handles to manually draw ease-in and ease-out curves.

  • Auto Curve (c): The software automatically calculates a smooth, spline-based transition.

  • Additional Tools: This menu also allows you to Simplify (reduce unnecessary keyframes), Quantize (snap keyframes to the grid), or manually Move Playhead Here.

 

Track Types & Inspectors

 

Clicking the + (Plus) button on a timeline allows you to add specific tracks to control different data streams. Each track type has its own specific context menus and inspector settings.

Timeline Player Tracks

Timeline Player Tracks allow you to directly arrange existing Scenes and Cues in a linear timeline based format.

 

 

 

Note: The Scenes and Cues will use the fades assigned to them under the Scenes and Cues tab or their individual timelines.

 

To add an existing Scene or Cue to a Timeline Player Track.  Simply double-click on the empty track and a box will pop up where you can search and select your individual Scenes and Cues.

 

When a scene is in the timeline, right-click on the clip to see more options.

 

Right-Click Clip Options: You can quickly Split Clip, Quantize, Copy/Cut, or navigate the playhead and loop brackets directly to the clip.

Montage Tracks

Brings non-linear editing directly into MadMapper. You can arrange, cut, snap, and time-reverse standard video and image content directly on the timeline.

 

You can arrange multiple montage tracks and route them to different sources (Layers, Lasers, DMX, etc.).  When you place two montage tracks next to each other, MadMapper will add a cross fade indicator that can be adjusted for different fade durations.

 

 

After you have created your montage track, they are available in the Media Bin for you to assign to other surfaces like any other media clip.

 

  • Media Bin Right-Click: Right-clicking a montage item in the bin allows you to Select surfaces using this media or Add to Timeline.

 

  • Clip Right-Click: On the timeline itself, right-clicking a movie clip allows you to Split Clip, Preview, Replace Visual, or Select all clips with same Visual.

 

 

  • Montage Inspector: Here you can view a live Preview of the track. You can set the No Media Behavior (choosing whether empty track space causes the surface to Skip Rendering entirely, or render solid Black) and choose to Force Media Resolution.

 

 

Audio Tracks

Drop an audio file into the timeline for visual synchronization, FFT frequency analysis, or Automated BeatTracking to drive generative visuals.

 

When an audio track is in the timeline, you can use the show inspector icon in the right side of the timeline window to make visual adjustments and changes to the audio routing.

 

 

  • Right-Click on the Clip: Standard arrangement options including Split Clip and Quantize.

 

  • Audio Clip Inspector: Controls parameters specific to the selected segment of audio. You can view the precise Time, Duration, and Start Offset. You can also manage the File reference, adjust Clip Gain, change the Clip Speed percentage, and view the Detected BPM.

 

 

  • Audio Track Inspector: Controls global settings for the entire track. You can adjust the master Track Gain and toggle the visual Preview between a Spectrum analyzer or standard Waveform.

 

Examples of Waveform vs Spectrum:

 

  • Background & Routing: In the Track Inspector, you can toggle Use as Background to keep the audio running beneath other operations, and utilize the Audio Routing matrix to send specific track channels to specific hardware outputs.

OSC Tracks

Sequence network commands to drive external lighting consoles or show control systems.

 

  • Data Types: When creating the track, choose between Float, Integer, String, Color, Bool, or Events.

  • OSC Inspector: Define the target OSC Device, write the exact OSC Address (e.g., /int-1), and establish the Min Value and Max Value boundaries for the automation. (Note: Clicking the Three Dots will open the main project preferences for network routing).

MIDI Tracks

Send sequenced control data to external hardware or instruments.

 

  • Data Types: When creating the track, choose between standard Control Change (CC), High Resolution CC (14 bits), Pitch Bend, or specific musical Notes.

  • MIDI Inspector: Define the target MIDI Device and select the outbound Channel (1-16). (Note: Clicking the Three Dots will open the main project preferences for MIDI routing).

Time Markers & Follow Actions

Markers allow you to add interactive logic to an otherwise linear timeline, creating complex loops or wait states. This comes in handy for shows where you want to hold at a pause point until you hit GO / (play button) to continue playing forward in the timeline. You can add a Marker to the top ruler and customize it in the Inspector.

Note: You can tell what type of marker is in the timeline based on the Prefix. P/ = Pause, L/ = Loop, G/ = Go to Marker.

 

Click the Flag icon to add a marker:

 

  • Marker Display: Color-code your markers and choose to display their exact location in Seconds, Frames, or Time Code using the Three Dots menu.

 

  • Manual Actions: The Inspector provides Go and Go and Play buttons to manually jump the playhead to that specific marker during a live show.

 

  • Default Actions: Define what happens automatically when the playhead naturally hits the marker. Options include Pause (wait for user input), Continue (ignore the marker and keep playing), Loop (return to a previous point), or Go to Marker.

 

 

  • Follow Actions: Program secondary logic chains by adding a Follow Action (e.g., instructing the timeline to jump to "Marker 1", or to execute a sequence like Go to Marker and Pause or Start Timeline).

Clips    

Clips are short, repeatable segments created independently from the main sequence. If you bring a video file into your Montage for editing, cut an in and out point, then right-click > create clip. MadMapper will now treat this clip like it's an isolated 'clip'.

 

After creating and selecting the clip, you will then have options under the Media Inspector to Enable Looping, adjust the clip Speed, and Modify the In & Out points of the clip itself.

 

Exporting a Timeline from the Conductor

MadMapper allows you to render and export your fully programmed timeline directly from the Conductor. This feature lets you bounce your synchronized video, audio, laser, and DMX sequences into standard files for playback on other systems, archiving, or sharing with clients.

To access these settings, navigate to your Conductor timeline and select the export option.

Export Dialogue Box

At the very top of the Export Timeline dialog, you must choose how much of your timeline you want to render:

  • Export until last key frame / marker: Renders the timeline from the very beginning up to the exact moment of the final programmed event, keyframe, or marker.

  • Export Loop section: Renders only the specific segment of time defined by the active loop brackets on your Conductor timeline.

Export Video Outputs

This section allows you to render your mapped video outputs into standard video files or image sequences.

  • Target Outputs: Select exactly which video outputs you want to render by checking their respective boxes (e.g., Video-Output-1).

  • Include Audio: Check this box next to an output to embed the timeline's audio mix directly into that resulting video file.

  • Quality Slider: Use this to balance file size and visual fidelity when using compressed formats like H.264.

Available Video Codecs:

  • H264 & HEVC: Standard compressed formats, ideal for sharing previews or web delivery.

  • ProRes: High-quality Apple codec, excellent for visually lossless editing and playback on macOS.

  • Hap, HapAlpha, HapQ: GPU-accelerated formats optimized for multi-layer live performance software.

  • Image Sequence: Exports every single frame of your timeline as an individual image file.

Export Laser & DMX Outputs

If your project contains hardware control data, you can export these specialized streams alongside your video.

  • ILDA Export (Laser Data): Bounces your programmed laser paths and generative animations into a standard ILDA movie file.

    • Compatibility: Because it writes to the universal ILDA standard, this exported file is fully compatible with any third-party laser control software that supports ILDA movies (such as Pangolin BEYOND or standard show controllers).

    • High-Resolution Vectorization: As noted in the Expert Mode settings, utilizing the Timeline export allows you to bypass real-time hardware limitations, enabling you to process massive video vectorization tasks (up to 16k resolution) into flawless ILDA sequences.

  • DMX Export (Lighting Data): Renders your lighting programming into a highly optimized, proprietary MadLight Sequence. (Note: Because this is a proprietary format, these files cannot be imported into third-party lighting consoles).

    • Delta Compression: To keep file sizes highly efficient, the export stores all of your DMX universes together but only records the changes in value over time. The data is then automatically zipped.

    • File Chunking: The software automatically cuts the export into smaller file chunks. This prevents the export from hitting the standard 32-bit file size limits found on FAT32-formatted USB drives.

    • Optimized Scrubbing: By splitting the export into smaller files, the time-offset index is built directly into the filenames rather than requiring a massive index at the beginning of a single file. This allows for incredibly fast timeline scrubbing and ensures smooth, low-overhead playback on lightweight standalone hardware (such as Raspberry Pi-based media players).

Export Audio Output

If you need an isolated audio mixdown of your timeline, enable the audio export section.

  • Audio Codec: Choose between uncompressed WAV for the highest fidelity, or compressed MP3 and M4A formats for smaller file sizes.

  • Audio Channels: Select the number of audio channels (e.g., 2 for a standard stereo mix).

  • Sample Rate: Define the audio resolution (e.g., 44100 Hz for standard CD quality).

Setting the Destination

At the bottom of the window, verify the Export Folder path. This is the directory on your hard drive where all selected video, audio, ILDA, and DMX files will be generated once you click OK. You can use the browse button on the right to designate a specific folder, or click the reset icon to return to the default MadMapper workspace directory.

Writing Custom GLSL Materials 

MadMapper Materials are generative, animated visuals rendered directly on the screen by your computer's GPU. While you can use the Mad AI extension to generate materials using text prompts, you also have the ability to write or modify the raw GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language) code yourself.

MadMapper Materials are based on the standard ISF (Interactive Shader Format) specification. However, because they are rendered directly onto MadMapper's output surfaces (Quads, 3D Surfaces, Lines, Fixtures) rather than just a flat texture, MadMapper utilizes a specific boilerplate and offers several powerful custom extensions.

 

See the GLSL Shader Functions Reference for more code examples.

Accessing the Code Editor

Writing code in the editor is very similar to using Mad AI to create a new shader.

  1. Navigate to the Media Bin and open the Materials section.

  2. Click the + (Plus) button to create a new material.

  3. You can either start with a blank material, or if you are using Mad AI, you can toggle directly from the AI interface over to the raw Code Editor to manually tweak the math the AI generated.

Check out the MadAI Extension documentation to get up and running quickly.

The Basic Boilerplate

Unlike a standard GLSL shader that uses a "void main" function, MadMapper fragment shaders require you to implement a specific function called "materialColorForPixel". This function must return a vec4 color based on a 2D texture coordinate.

 

Here is the most basic boilerplate for a MadMapper material:

 

OpenGL Shading Language
 
/*{
    "CREDIT": "Your Name",
    "TAGS": "Generative, Custom",
    "INPUTS": []
}*/

// texCoord is the texture coordinate (position in the input media for this pixel)
vec4 materialColorForPixel(vec2 texCoord) {
    // Returns a solid red color (Red, Green, Blue, Alpha)
    return vec4(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); 
}

Exposing UI Parameters (Inputs)

To control your shader live, you can declare INPUTS inside the JSON header block at the top of your file. MadMapper will automatically read this JSON and build the corresponding sliders, buttons, and color pickers in the Inspector.

  • Naming Convention: Always start your variable names with "mat_" (e.g., mat_speed or mat_color). This prevents your variables from conflicting with MadMapper's internal Surface FX code.

  • Supported Types: You can create parameters of type float, int, bool (checkbox), color, and floatRange (a min/max slider).

  • UI Flags: You can alter how the UI looks using the FLAGS parameter. For example, assigning "FLAGS": "button" to a boolean turns the checkbox into a push-button. Assigning "FLAGS": "no_alpha" to a color input removes the transparency slider.

  • Grouping: You can organize your parameters into clean folders in the Inspector by adding a forward slash to the LABEL. For example, "LABEL": "Noise/Speed" will put the Speed slider inside a "Noise" group.

 

Example of an Input Variable:

 

JSON
 
{
    "LABEL": "Global/My Speed",
    "NAME": "mat_speed",
    "TYPE": "float",
    "MIN": 0.0,
    "MAX": 1.0,
    "DEFAULT": 0.5
}

Built-In Variables & Macros

MadMapper automatically provides several global variables to your shader, following the ISF specification:

  • TIME: The elapsed time in seconds.

  • TIMEDELTA: The time passed since the last frame.

  • RENDERSIZE: The dimensions of the output (Note: this is only valid if you enable "Render to Texture" in the material settings, as standard materials do not have a fixed pixel resolution).

Example: Using TIME for animation and RENDERSIZE for pixel-perfect math.

 

OpenGL Shading Language
 
/*{
    "CREDIT": "MadMapper User",
    "TAGS": "Variables",
    "INPUTS": []
}*/

vec4 materialColorForPixel(vec2 texCoord) {
    // 1. TIME: Create a pulsing value between 0.0 and 1.0
    float pulse = (sin(TIME * 3.0) + 1.0) * 0.5;
    
    // 2. RENDERSIZE: Get the exact pixel coordinate 
    // (Note: "Render to Texture" MUST be enabled for this to work!)
    vec2 pixelCoord = texCoord * RENDERSIZE;
    
    // Draw a color that shifts based on the pulse
    vec3 color = vec3(texCoord.x, texCoord.y, pulse);
    
    return vec4(color, 1.0);
}

 

Audio Reactivity

You can easily pass audio data directly into your shader code using the audioFFT (spectrum) or audio (waveform) input types. MadMapper allows you to define the SIZE of the frequency bands and apply internal ATTACK, DECAY, and RELEASE smoothing filters directly in the JSON header.

Example: Creating a 16-band spectrum analyzer with built-in attack/decay smoothing.

 

OpenGL Shading Language
 
/*{
    "CREDIT": "MadMapper User",
    "TAGS": "Audio Reactive",
    "INPUTS": [
        {
            "NAME": "mat_spectrum",
            "TYPE": "audioFFT",
            "SIZE": 16,
            "ATTACK": 0.05,
            "DECAY": 0.2,
            "RELEASE": 0.1
        }
    ]
}*/

vec4 materialColorForPixel(vec2 texCoord) {
    // Audio textures are 1D (height is always 1 pixel).
    // We sample the spectrum using the built-in IMG_NORM_PIXEL macro.
    // We use texCoord.x to sweep across the frequency bands.
    float audioValue = IMG_NORM_PIXEL(mat_spectrum, vec2(texCoord.x, 0.5)).r;
    
    // If our Y coordinate is below the audio volume, draw green. Otherwise, draw black.
    vec3 color = texCoord.y < audioValue ? vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.5) : vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
    
    return vec4(color, 1.0);
}

Generators (Solving the "TIME" Problem)

If you animate a shape by multiplying TIME by a user-controlled mat_speed slider, changing the speed live will cause the animation to jump wildly (because the total multiplier suddenly shifts).

To solve this, MadMapper introduced Generators. Instead of doing the math in GLSL, you declare a time_base generator in your JSON header. MadMapper will calculate a smooth, continuously increasing value based on your speed, and pass that perfect value into your shader as a variable.

Generators can also be synced perfectly to the application's global tempo by setting "bpm_sync": true.

Example: Using a time_base generator synced to the global BPM to drive a smooth animation, rather than directly multiplying TIME.

 

OpenGL Shading Language
 
/*{
    "CREDIT": "MadMapper User",
    "TAGS": "Generators",
    "INPUTS": [
        {
            "LABEL": "Animation Speed",
            "NAME": "mat_speed",
            "TYPE": "float",
            "MIN": 0.0,
            "MAX": 2.0,
            "DEFAULT": 1.0
        }
    ],
    "GENERATORS": [
        {
            "NAME": "mat_anim_time",
            "TYPE": "time_base",
            "PARAMS": {
                "speed": "mat_speed",
                "bpm_sync": true
            }
        }
    ]
}*/

vec4 materialColorForPixel(vec2 texCoord) {
    // Instead of doing: sin(TIME * mat_speed)
    // We use the perfectly generated 'mat_anim_time' variable!
    float smoothAnimation = (sin(mat_anim_time) + 1.0) * 0.5;
    
    return vec4(vec3(smoothAnimation), 1.0);
}

 

Included Libraries

MadMapper bundles highly optimized open-source math libraries directly into the software. You do not need to write complex noise algorithms from scratch; simply include them at the top of your shader code (after the JSON header) using standard include statements.

  • MadCommon: Provides constants like PI, and essential color conversion functions like rgb2hsv and hsv2rgb.

  • MadNoise: Provides incredibly powerful 2D and 3D noises, including vnoise, simplex noise, worleyNoise, flowNoise, fBm (Fractal Brownian Motion), and curlNoise.

  • MadSDF: Provides a library of Signed Distance Field math, making it exceptionally easy to draw crisp 2D shapes mathematically.

Example: Using MadNoise for generative textures and MadCommon to convert Hue, Saturation, and Value into an RGB color.

 

OpenGL Shading Language
 
/*{
    "CREDIT": "MadMapper User",
    "TAGS": "Libraries",
    "INPUTS": []
}*/

// Include statements must go AFTER the JSON header and BEFORE your functions
#include "MadCommon.glsl"
#include "MadNoise.glsl"
#include "MadSDF.glsl"

vec4 materialColorForPixel(vec2 texCoord) {
    // 1. Use MadNoise to create a 3D simplex noise 
    // We pass it our X/Y coordinates and TIME for the Z axis so it evolves
    float n = noise(vec3(texCoord * 5.0, TIME * 0.5));
    
    // 2. Use MadCommon's hsv2rgb function
    // We slowly shift the Hue based on TIME, while keeping saturation and value at 1.0
    vec3 rainbowColor = hsv2rgb(vec3(TIME * 0.1, 1.0, 1.0));
    
    // Multiply our rainbow by our noise
    return vec4(rainbowColor * n, 1.0);
}

Here is the fully commented code, breaking down exactly what each section of the shader is doing. I have formatted it under a new heading so you can drop it directly at the bottom of your Chapter 14 documentation page.

Complete Example: The Dunes Shader

Below is a complete, real-world example of a MadMapper Material. This shader creates a flowing, wavy dune pattern. We have heavily commented the code so you can see exactly how the JSON header, custom math functions, and the main materialColorForPixel function work together to create the final visual.

 

OpenGL Shading Language
 
/*{
    "CREDIT": "Mad Team",
    "DESCRIPTION": "Dunes.",
    "VSN": "1.0",
    "TAGS": "graphic",
    
    // ---------------------------------------------------------
    // 1. INPUTS: These create the UI controls in MadMapper
    // ---------------------------------------------------------
    "INPUTS": [
        // Creates a slider for zooming in/out
        { "LABEL": "Scale", "NAME": "scale", "TYPE": "float", "DEFAULT": 1.0, "MIN": 0.0, "MAX": 4.0 },
        
        // Creates a slider for animation speed
        { "LABEL": "Speed", "NAME": "speed", "TYPE": "float", "MIN" : 0.0, "MAX" : 4.0, "DEFAULT": 1.0 },
        
        // Creates a push-button to reverse the animation direction
        { "LABEL": "Reverse", "NAME": "reverse", "TYPE": "bool", "DEFAULT": false, "FLAGS": "button" },
        
        // Creates a color picker for the dune lines
        { "LABEL": "Color/Front Color", "NAME": "foregroundColor", "TYPE": "color", "DEFAULT": [ 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 ] },  
        
        // Creates sliders for brightness and contrast
        { "LABEL": "Color/Brightness", "NAME": "brightness", "TYPE": "float", "MIN": -1.0, "MAX": 1.0, "DEFAULT": 0 },
        { "LABEL": "Color/Contrast", "NAME": "contrast", "TYPE": "float", "MIN": 1.0, "MAX": 3.0, "DEFAULT": 1 },
    ],
    
    // ---------------------------------------------------------
    // 2. GENERATORS: Smoothly handling time and speed
    // ---------------------------------------------------------
    "GENERATORS": [
        // This generates a variable called 'animation_time'. 
        // It uses the 'speed' and 'reverse' inputs to calculate a smooth time value, 
        // preventing the animation from jumping when the user drags the speed slider.
        // It also links this animation directly to MadMapper's global BPM.
        { "NAME": "animation_time", "TYPE": "time_base", "PARAMS": {"speed": "speed", "reverse": "reverse", "speed_curve": 3, "link_speed_to_global_bpm":true} }
    ]
}*/

// ---------------------------------------------------------
// 3. MATH & NOISE FUNCTIONS
// Because shaders calculate everything mathematically per-pixel, 
// we use procedural formulas to generate random numbers and noise.
// ---------------------------------------------------------

// A hashing function that takes a 2D coordinate and returns a pseudo-random 2D vector.
vec2 hash( vec2 p ) {
  p = vec2(dot(p,vec2(127.1,311.7)),
           dot(p,vec2(269.5,183.3)));
  return -1. + 2.*fract(sin(p+20.)*53758.5453123);
}

// A 2D noise function based on the hash above. 
// It smooths out the random numbers to create organic, cloud-like values.
float dunes_noise( in vec2 x ) {
  vec2 p = floor(x);
  vec2 f = fract(x);
  f = f*f*(3.0-2.0*f);
  vec2 uv = (p+vec2(37.0,17.0)) + f;
  vec2 rg = hash( uv/256.0 ).yx;
  return 0.5*mix( rg.x, rg.y, 0.5 );
}

// A simple wrapper function to easily get a random float using two integers
float rnd(int i, int j) {
  return dunes_noise(vec2(i, j));
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------
// 4. THE PATTERN GENERATOR (Gabor Noise)
// ---------------------------------------------------------
#define GABOR_BLOBS_NB 10       // How many overlapping waves to create
#define GABOR_BLOBS_SIZE 0.25   // The size of each wave

// This function creates the actual "Dune" look by layering multiple sine waves 
// (blobs) moving in slightly different random directions.
float DuneStripes (vec2 uv, float d, float freq, float time) {
  float hv = 0.;
  
  // Loop through and create 10 different blobs
  for (int i=0; i<GABOR_BLOBS_NB; i++) {
    // Give each blob a random position and direction
    vec2 pos = vec2(rnd(i,0), rnd(i,1));
    vec2 dir = (.15+d)*vec2(rnd(i,2),rnd(i,3)) - d;
    
    // Add this blob's mathematical wave to our total height value (hv)
    hv += GABOR_BLOBS_SIZE * sin(dot(uv-pos, freq*dir) * 6. + time);
  }
  
  // Return the final combined wave pattern
  return hv;
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------
// 5. THE MAIN FUNCTION
// This is executed for every single pixel on the surface.
// ---------------------------------------------------------
vec4 materialColorForPixel(vec2 texCoord) {
    
  // Step A: Coordinate Setup
  // Center the coordinates around 0.5, apply the user's Scale slider, 
  // and then shift them back. This zooms the pattern in and out from the center.
  vec2 uv = vec2(0.5,0.5) + (texCoord-vec2(0.5,0.5)) * scale;
  
  // Step B: Generate the Pattern
  // Call our DuneStripes function using the scaled coordinates.
  // We pass in our perfectly smooth 'animation_time' generator to make it move!
  float h = DuneStripes(uv, -.5, 10.0, -3.5 * animation_time);
  
  // Step C: Apply Color
  // Multiply the user's chosen Foreground Color by our dune pattern (h).
  // clamp() ensures the brightness values don't drop below 0.0 or exceed 1.0.
  vec3 color = foregroundColor.rgb * clamp(h, 0.0, 1.0);

  // Step D: Apply Contrast
  // mix() blends between a flat gray (vec3(0.5)) and our current color based on the Contrast slider.
  color = mix(vec3(0.5), color, contrast);

  // Step E: Apply Brightness
  // Simply add or subtract the brightness slider value from the final color.
  color += vec3(brightness);

  // Step F: Output the Pixel
  // Return the final calculated color, with an Alpha (transparency) of 1.0 (fully opaque).
  return vec4(color, 1.0);
}

Special Tools & Auto-Calibration

When dealing with highly complex stages, scattered LED installations, or intricate architectural mappings, manual calibration can become incredibly time-consuming. MadMapper provides three powerful auto-calibration tools to speed up these advanced workflows.

These features can be accessed from the top menu bar under Tools -> Scanners: Space Scanner, LED Scanner, and Laser Scanner.

Space Scanner

(Formerly the Spatial Scanner)

If you do not have a pre-built 3D model of your stage or building, you can use the Space Scanner to accurately calibrate your projector's perspective relative to your physical scene.

Understanding the Process

The Space Scanner does not create a 3D model. Instead, it projects a series of structured light patterns (black and white stripes) from your projector, which are captured by your camera. By analyzing how these patterns distort across your physical surfaces, MadMapper calculates the exact perspective of the projector's lens. The result is a high-resolution, pixel-perfect "calibration map" that you can use as a background layer while you work on your mappings.

Note: These background calibration layers are used to guide your workflow and do not have to appear in your final output.

Setup & Configuration

  1. Open the Scanner: Access the tool via Tools > Scanners > Space Scanner.

  2. Select Hardware: In the top toolbar, select your Source (webcam, USB camera, or supported Canon DSLR) and the Projector output.

  3. Adjust Timing: Set your Capture Timing to ensure the camera shutter is synchronized with the projected patterns.

  4. Execute Capture: Click Capture to begin the automated sequence.

Best Practices for Accuracy

To ensure the most accurate calibration, please follow these guidelines:

  • Lens Alignment: Place your camera lens as close to the projector's lens as possible.

  • Stability: Once the process begins, do not move the camera or the projector.

  • Clearance: Ensure no people or objects move in front of the projection during the scan, as any movement will skew the final image calculation.

 

LED Scanner

When building custom LED installations, placing physical light tubes or pixel tape rarely results in a perfect geometric grid. Trying to manually arrange dozens of virtual DMX fixtures in MadMapper to match their scattered real-world positions is notoriously difficult. The LED Scanner automates this entirely.

Setup & Configuration

  1. Position the Camera: Position a camera (webcam or DSLR) so it has a clear view of your entire physical LED installation.

  2. Open the Scanner: Access the LED Scanner via Tools > Scanners > LED Scanner.

  3. Configure Parameters: In the LED Scanner panel, define the following settings:

    • Camera: Select the input device (e.g., FaceTime HD Camera).

    • Fixture Definition: Choose the specific profile (e.g., GarageCube - SFX-01 RGB 1m).

    • DMX Range: Define the Start Universe/Channel and End Universe/Channel that the scanner should monitor for your LED installation.

    • Brightness & Threshold: Adjust these sliders to ensure the camera can clearly distinguish the flashing LEDs from the ambient light in the room.

    • Map LEDs at 0,0 if not detected: An optional safety check to catch any pixels that were missed during the scan.

  4. The Scan: Click Start Scan. MadMapper will sequentially flash every single LED pixel in your physical installation one by one.

  5. The Result: The camera tracks these flashes in real-time. Once finished, MadMapper automatically arranges all of your virtual DMX fixtures in your MadLight workspace to perfectly mirror their exact physical coordinates in the real world. You can immediately drop a video texture across your workspace, and it will map flawlessly across your physical LEDs.

 

Laser Scanner

Introduced in MadMapper 5.5, the Laser Scanner brings the power of auto-calibration to the MadLaser extension.

Because laser hardware utilizes high-speed mechanical galvanometers (mirrors) rather than pixel grids, aligning laser paths to physical architecture or syncing them perfectly over a video projection traditionally requires intensive, manual Bezier warping.

By utilizing the Laser Scanner, a connected camera reads calibration patterns drawn by your physical laser projector. The software calculates the exact physical distortion, angle, and distance of the laser beam, and automatically generates a corrected mapping. This ensures that your vector paths, ILDA files, and laser materials hit your physical targets with absolute precision.

Using the Laser Scanner

To use the Laser Scanner, you must first have your laser configured properly. If the laser is armed and capable of outputting an image from MadMapper, you can enable the Laser Scanner, which will create a 16x16 matrix of laser dots.

Similar to the Space Scanner, the Laser Scanner will capture images as the rows and columns of dots move. It is crucial that the camera and laser projector do not move during this process. When completed, the Laser Scanner tool will interpret the information and create a custom background image. You will be asked to choose a name and destination for this image, and then it will be automatically displayed in your laser canvas.

 

The image generated will not appear on the final laser output.

DMX & LED Mapping

MadMapper is not just a video tool; its integrated MadLight engine allows you to seamlessly bridge the gap between video pixels and physical lighting. Whether you are mapping a few RGB tubes, complex architectural moving heads, or a massive pixel-mapped stage design, the DMX features allow you to translate your visual compositions directly into physical light.

DMX Fundamentals

Before patching fixtures, it is important to understand how MadMapper communicates with your physical lighting hardware.

 

DMX Preferences: To route your lighting data, navigate to Preferences > Project (tab) > DMX. Here you can select your network interface, choose your USB DMX device, Art-Net or sACN, and define your framerate to ensure smooth playback across your rig.

 

  • DMX512: The standard lighting control protocol. A single DMX cable can carry 512 channels of data. This bundle of 512 channels is called a Universe. For example, a standard RGB LED pixel uses 3 channels (Red, Green, Blue). Therefore, one DMX universe can control up to 170 individual RGB pixels (170 x 3 = 510). If you are controlling lights that go beyond 512 channels, then they will stretch over onto a new universe. Some external hardware devices are limited to output over a single universe, while others can output over 96 universes through a single device.

  • Art-Net & sACN: Because large LED installations often require tens of thousands of channels, routing physical DMX cables for every universe is impossible. Art-Net and sACN are network protocols that send massive amounts of DMX universes over standard Ethernet cables. MadMapper outputs these protocols to network nodes (like PixLite, Advatek, or Enttec boxes), which then translate the data back into physical DMX or SPI signals for your lights.

Current hardware supported by MadMapper are the following USB DMX Devices: garageCube, ShowJockey, Enttec DMX USB Pro, Enttec DMX USB Pro MK2, and the DMX King eDMX2 Pro, and network based devices that support Art-Net or sACN.

 

Output Configuration: To route your lighting data, navigate to Preferences > Project (tab) > DMX. Here you can select your network interface, choose your USB DMX device, Art-Net or sACN, and define your framerate to ensure smooth playback across your rig.

DMX Filtering

DMX Filtering controls how MadMapper samples the video content for your lighting fixtures. Applying a filter averages the surrounding pixels, which helps prevent harsh flickering when playing high-contrast video over low-resolution LEDs.

  • None: Samples a single, exact pixel at the center of the fixture.
  • Box: Averages a square grid of pixels around the sample point (defined by the Size parameter).
  • Anamorphic: Averages an area with independent width and height parameters (X and Y), which is perfect for mapping rectangular LED strips or non-square pixels.

Option Description

Mapping Modes

  • Fixed Size: Manually set the pixel grid dimensions (Width × Height). In this mode, you can customize the individual pixel patch by clicking directly on any pixel in the Pixel Mapping interface to toggle it between its DMX address and UNPATCHED.

Fixture Properties & Mapping

The Properties panel allows you to define the geometric structure of your fixture, while the Pixel Mapping interface gives you granular control over individual pixel addressing.

 

Pixel Type — Select the color model for the fixture's pixels: RGB, RGBW, or Custom (for non-standard channel layouts like the IVL Dice).

Pixel Size — The number of DMX channels per pixel (e.g., 3 for RGB, 4 for RGBW). Check Advanced to access per-channel type and label configuration.

Assignation — Defines the pixel scanning/addressing order for LED strips and matrices. The 16 arrow pattern icons represent different ways pixels can be wired through the grid: left-to-right then top-to-bottom (Z-pattern), serpentine/zigzag, bottom-to-top, column-first, and their mirrored and reversed variants. Select the pattern that matches how your LEDs are physically wired. Click Clear to reset.

Skip channels 511–512 — When enabled, MadMapper will leave DMX channels 511 and 512 empty at the end of each universe. Some DMX devices reserve these channels, and enabling this avoids addressing conflicts at universe boundaries.

Channel Types

Each channel in a fixture definition has a type that tells MadMapper how to interpret it:

Type Description Typical Use
R Red RGB/RGBW color mixing
G Green RGB/RGBW color mixing
B Blue RGB/RGBW color mixing
W White RGBW fixtures
L Luminance Single-channel brightness
C Cyan CMY color mixing
M Magenta CMY color mixing
Y Yellow CMY color mixing
Slider Generic DMX value (0–255) Dimmer, pan, tilt, speed, gobo, or any non-color channel with manual control
Expression GLSL expression Computed channel value driven by a formula (see Expression Channels below)
Unused Empty/skipped channel Placeholder for reserved or unneeded channels in the fixture's DMX footprint

Bit Depth

Channels can be set to 8 Bits (single channel, 0–255) or 16 Bits (two channels, coarse + fine, 0–65535). 

 

Expression Channels

Expression channels let you compute a DMX value using a GLSL expression instead of a fixed slider or color input. This is useful for deriving channel values from other parameters — for example, calculating a checksum, inverting a value, or mixing multiple inputs mathematically.

 

The following variables are available inside an expression:

Variable Description
R, G, B Current red, green, and blue color values
L Luminance value
W White value
C, M, Y Cyan, magenta, and yellow values
INDEX The pixel index within the fixture
posX, posY Normalized pixel position within the fixture grid
COMP Component index
time Current time value
Slider names The values of any Slider channels, referenced by their label name

Expressions follow GLSL syntax, so standard math functions like sin(), clamp(), mix(), step(), etc. are available.

Controlling Moving Lights

MadMapper's fixture engine is not limited to LED strips; it is fully capable of driving intelligent fixtures, moving heads, and complex DMX devices (like fog machines or the Minuit Une IVL Dice), but the logic you are used to to control the devices will be slightly different from traditional DMX consoles.

Instead of relying on a traditional programmer with faders and palettes for every parameter, MadMapper drives the color and intensity of the fixture by sampling your video content, while generating custom UI sliders for the mechanical features.

To control moving lights:

  1. Create a custom fixture definition with a 1x1 pixel grid.
  2. Set the Pixel Type to Custom.
  3. Map the manufacturer's DMX sheet to the channels. Assign the color parameters to R, G, B types (so they sample the video map).
  4. Assign the Pan, Tilt, Strobe, and Gobo parameters to the Slider type.
  5. In your MadMapper workspace, these Sliders will now appear in the Fixture Inspector, allowing you to manually aim the moving heads while their colors dynamically react to your video content!

Tip: After you have created a slider, you can animate it with keyframes in the Timelines tab, or connect it to Oscillator modules created under the Modules tab to generate automatic, continuous movement.

Real-World Example: PAR 6-Channel

For standard pixel mapping with addressable RGB LED pixels, a fixture will not require a complex definition. But this example shows how MadMapper fixtures can be customized to work with non-standard fixtures like an LED PAR can with additional color diodes, such as Amber and UV (Ultraviolet).

This fixture is a 6-channel LED PAR. It uses a 1×1 pixel grid with the Pixel Type set to "Custom" and a Pixel Size of 6 channels. The first four channels are assigned to standard color types (R, G, B, and W) so they can directly sample the video map. The remaining two channels are dedicated to the Amber and UV diodes.

By setting these last two channels to the "Slider" type and labeling them "Amber" and "UV", MadMapper automatically generates dedicated sliders for them at the bottom of the Fixture Inspector. This allows the operator to manually mix in Amber and UV light independently while the main RGBW channels dynamically react to the video content.

Tips for Custom Fixtures

Naming conventions — Use clear, descriptive channel labels. Include "Fine" in the label for the LSB channel of 16-bit pairs so operators can quickly identify coarse/fine relationships.

Modes — Many fixtures have multiple DMX modes with different channel counts. Create a separate definition for each mode and include the mode in the product name (e.g., "Minuit Une IVL Dice Mode 1").

Testing — After creating a fixture definition, use the DMX Monitor panel (Option+Cmd+M / Alt+Ctrl+M) to verify that channels are mapping correctly and values are reaching the expected DMX addresses.

Color channel types — Use the correct R/G/B/W/C/M/Y types for color channels rather than Slider. This allows MadMapper's color engine to properly drive them with pixel-mapped media, materials, and color pickers.

Cross-universe fixtures — If your fixture spans more than 512 channels or if its DMX address places it near the end of a universe, enable avoidCrossUniversePixels to prevent a single pixel's channels from being split across two universes.

Backup — Keep your custom .mmfl files in a shared location or version control. Fixture definitions are stored within MadMapper's library, but having external backups ensures you can quickly rebuild on a new machine.
