Soft-Edge Blending

When you need to cover a massive physical canvas, a single projector is rarely enough. Soft-edge blending allows you to overlap the output of multiple projectors and smoothly fade their intersecting edges, creating a single, massive, seamless image.

Note: Soft-Edge blending only applies to Quads. Laser Soft-Edge Blending is a similar process.

Understanding Projector Overlap

  • The "Sweet Spot": For standard edge blending in MadMapper, aim for an overlap of approximately 10% to 20%. If you are using MadMapper's official calibration card, this visually translates to overlapping about four grid boxes in the center.
  • Why Overlap Matters: Without a soft edge, the intersecting area of two projectors is twice as bright (creating a harsh "hot spot"). MadMapper uses this shared physical space to calculate a smooth gradient fade, dimming each projector's edge proportionally so the transition is invisible.
  • Balancing Canvas Size vs. Tolerance: A larger overlap gives you more visual tolerance if a projector vibrates or gets slightly bumped during a live event. However, keep in mind that every pixel in the overlap zone is "double-duty" data—meaning the more your projectors overlap, the smaller your total physical canvas width becomes.
  • Projector Stacking (100% Overlap): If your goal is not to create a wider image, but rather a brighter image, you can overlap the projectors 100%. MadMapper easily handles stacking by simply duplicating the output mapping across both projectors to double the luminance.

Best Practices & Setup Tips

  • Match Your Hardware: Using the exact same projector model with a similar bulb life is highly recommended. Mixing models or bulb ages will cause issues with inaccurate colors, mismatched resolutions, and uneven lamp brightness that cannot be easily fixed in software.
  • Physical Alignment First: Before attempting software edge blending, try to physically align your projectors and mechanically adjust their keystone and lens shift as perfectly as possible to make the software process much easier.
  • Lens Considerations: Standard lenses are best for edge blending. Short Throw and Ultra-Short Throw (UST) lenses can be much more difficult to blend because of how drastically the extreme edges of the lens warp the image projection.
Written by ProjectileObjects

Standard Technique: Built-In Soft Edge

The standard blending method uses MadMapper's automated soft-edge tools to feather the top, bottom, left, or right edges of your video quads.

  1. Output Setup: In the Projectors tab, ensure both projectors are enabled, set to fullscreen mode, and visually check their position by temporarily activating their built-in test patterns.
  2. Calibration Media: Add a calibration card to your Media Bin (these can be downloaded from the MadMapper website). Assign this media to a Quad and duplicate the Quad for your second projector.
  3. Physical Overlap: In the stage view, arrange your Quads so they overlap to form a larger rectangle. The physical projection should overlap by approximately 10% to 20% (or roughly four boxes if using a standard grid calibration card).
  4. Geometric Alignment: Adjust the four corner handles of each Quad in the output view so the overlapping grid boxes perfectly match and align in the real world.
  5. Auto Setup: Select both Quads in your Surfaces list at the same time. In the Surface Inspector, check the Soft Edge box and click the Auto Setup button. MadMapper will automatically calculate the intersecting areas and apply a gradient fade. (Note: For the "Auto Setup" calibration to work, you must select multiple surfaces simultaneously).
  6. Fine Tuning: Select each Quad individually and expand the Soft Edge parameters. You can manually adjust the Width and Power (gamma curve) of the blend on the overlapping side (e.g., adjust the right edge of the left projector, and the left edge of the right projector) until the seam disappears.

Advanced Technique: Blending with Surface Masks

The built-in Soft Edge tool only works on straight, perpendicular edges (top, left, bottom, and right). However, in complex projection mapping scenarios, your projectors may be overlapping at odd angles or projecting onto non-flat architecture where simple edge blending won't do.

For overlapping edges that are not parallel or perpendicular, you can create custom soft edges using Internal Masks:

  1. Select the Quad or Surface you need to blend.
  2. In the Surface Inspector, add a new Mask (or use the Mask tool to draw a shape over the specific area where the projectors overlap).
  3. Shape the internal mask to perfectly follow the contour of the intersecting projector light.
  4. Adjust the Feathering parameter on the mask. This will create a custom, variable gradient fade along the drawn line of the mask.
  5. Repeat this process for the intersecting surface on the second projector, and adjust both feathering values to achieve a smooth, custom edge blend.

Laser (MadLaser)

Getting Started with MadLaser

MadLaser Preferences

The foundational settings for laser output and safety are managed within the main MadMapper Preferences menu (Cmd + , on Mac / Ctrl + , on PC). Because lasers involve physical hardware and strict safety protocols, these settings are split between global application routing and project-specific safety limits.

Important Note: The settings detailed in the Laser tabs below are exclusive to the MadLaser extension. These menus and options will only appear in your preferences if the MadLaser extension is currently licensed and activated on your system.

Application Tab > Laser

These settings govern global audio-to-laser network protocols on your specific computer, regardless of which project file is open.

  • Enable Audio Laser (AVB / Dante): Check this box to allow MadMapper to send laser control data over standard audio network protocols.
  • Audio Device & Channels: Select your target network audio interface (e.g., NDI Audio, Dante Virtual Soundcard) and configure the Sample Rate, Buffer Size, and Audio Channels per Unit.
  • Enable Scene Markers: Toggles the transmission of scene markers over the audio network.

Project Tab > Laser

These settings contain critical safety and visualization parameters. Because they directly affect the physical output of the laser hardware, they are saved directly into your current .mad project file.

Security Settings
By default, MadMapper limits certain laser parameters to protect both your audience and your hardware.

  • Unlock Security Features: Checking this box prompts a warning regarding the dangers of high-intensity beams. Unlocking this allows you to bypass the default safety constraints.

  • Max non-moving Beam Intensity: MadMapper natively prevents static (non-moving) beams from outputting at full power. This slider dictates the maximum brightness allowed when the scanners stop moving.

Safety Warning: A full-power, static beam from a professional laser can easily ignite fires or burn skin. Never increase this limit unless you are absolutely certain the beam path is safely terminated and clear of the audience.

Enable Expert Mode Settings
Enabling Expert Mode in your Project Preferences unlocks advanced, under-the-hood parameters designed specifically for complex installations and high-end hardware.

Arming the Laser & Output Preparation

While you can design and preview your laser surfaces within the software workspace, no physical light will be emitted from your hardware until the system is armed. To see your image in the real world, you must arm the laser by toggling the Laser Output icon located in the upper right corner of the main MadMapper application window.

The Arming Warning: The first time you arm the laser output during a session, MadMapper will present a mandatory safety acknowledgment:

Please read this carefully. As the software explicitly states, you must not shoot rays towards your audience, you must comply with local regulations, and you should always use a physical safety switch (e-stop) on your hardware. Once you accept the prompt and the laser icon is activated, MadMapper will begin sending live vector data to your connected hardware.

 

Laser Outputs

With MadLaser you can create a large number of laser outputs and route them to multiple projectors in various ways. Using a form of Laser Dispatch you can spread complex content over multiple lasers with up to 100 kpps scanners for rendering high definition graphics.

 

Add laser icon:

To configure your laser, navigate to the Outputs tab and add a new laser. View the laser output inspector to configure the destination of your laser from the dropdown list.

Supported devices should automatically appear in the dropdown menu. These include:

  • ShowNET: The most seamless, plug-and-play integration. Lasers with a built-in ShowNET mainboard (such as models from the Laserworld Diode, Laserworld Purelight, Tarm, and Ray Technologies/RTI series) can connect directly via a standard LAN cable.

  • LaserCube: Recognized as one of the best and most portable plug-and-play options.

  • EtherDream: Highly supported for its 16-bit X/Y precision and network capabilities.

  • Helios USB: A popular, budget-friendly USB DAC.

  • FB3 / FB4 (Pangolin): Supported on Windows, though this requires an active Pangolin Beyond license.

  • AVB / Dante & IDN: Supported for networked environments and multi-projector setups.

Laser Surface Basics

Laser surfaces allow you to create and manage your laser outputs for your mapping projects. By adding laser surfaces, you define how shapes, generative content, or video textures are translated into real-time laser trajectories on your physical installation. Unlike standard video projection, MadMapper handles laser content in two distinct ways:

  • Native Laser Materials: Generative, shader-based materials (GLSL) that natively output mathematical vector data directly to the laser hardware. This circumvents the need for pixel-tracing, resulting in the sharpest, most scanner-efficient rendering possible.
  • Image Vectorization (Tracing): A GPU-accelerated, custom OpenCV engine that analyzes pixel-based media in real time. This allows you to trace contours and paths from movies, live camera inputs, or by sampling directly from your active video composition.

Location & Creation
Access the Laser surfaces by clicking on Laser at the top left of the interface (Shortcut: Cmd + 3). Simply click on the Laser surface of your choice in the top bar to add one.

Laser Surfaces List & Groups
Added Laser surfaces and groups will be listed on the left. You can toggle visibility, lock surfaces to prevent accidental edits, and drag surfaces into Groups to organize them by physical laser projectors.

 

 

Basic Surface Types

Laser Quad

This allows you to map vector graphics or vectorize video content within a four-point warped surface similar to a Video surface.

 

Laser Lines: Create precise, path-based line surfaces, perfect for tracing physical architecture. You can draw straight lines, Bezier curves, and split or link tangents for advanced point editing.



Laser Circle: Add circles, scale, and rotate them directly in the Stage View. Ideal for rounded architectural elements or geometric tunnels.

Laser Text: Create sharp, legible text generated as laser-optimized vector paths. Stick Fonts are highly recommended for laser use, as they trace a single line to reduce scanner flicker.


Laser Render Inspector

These are the advanced controls dictating how the software translates visual data into physical scanner movements.

  • Scan & Beam Mode: Set to Auto or manually configure.
  • Max Speed: Defines the maximum drawing speed of the laser.
  • Optimize Angles: When activated, utilizes the Angle Min, Angle Delay, and End Repeat parameters to instruct the laser scanners to dwell slightly on sharp corners, ensuring crisp geometry instead of rounded edges.
  • In Fade / Out Fade / Soft Close: Controls the blanking (turning the laser diode on/off) at the start and end of drawing paths to prevent visible tails or connecting lines.

ILDA Files

The ILDA format (.ild) is the universal standard for sharing and playing back pre-rendered laser graphics and animations. MadMapper fully supports importing and exporting ILDA files to integrate seamlessly with other laser workflows.

Importing ILDA Content

You can import .ild files directly into your Media Bin just like a standard video file. Once imported, simply drag and drop the ILDA file onto any active Laser Surface to play back the pre-rendered vector animation. Because ILDA files already contain exact X/Y coordinate and color data, they are incredibly efficient and bypass the need for real-time image tracing.

Exporting ILDA Content

If you use MadMapper's powerful generative engine to create custom laser shows, you can bake that content down into a static file for use on standalone media players or other laser software.

  • Via the Timeline: You can export sequences directly to ILDA via the Timeline export options.
  • High-Resolution Vectorization (Expert Mode): When Expert Mode is enabled, the video vectorization engine can process media up to 16k resolution. While real-time performance will degrade at 16k, this is an incredibly powerful feature for executing non-real-time conversions of massive video files into high-resolution ILDA exports.

Real-Time Video Vectorization

One of MadMapper's most powerful features is its ability to convert standard, pixel-based video content into physical laser vectors in real-time. This is handled primarily through the Laser Quad surface.

 

Process Inspector

This panel dictates how standard video is broken down and traced by the computer vision engine.

  • Set the Mode (e.g., Find Paths or Find Contours).
  • Adjust the tracing Threshold and toggle Use Color.
  • Refine the trace using Thickness, Denoizing, and Max Res to balance visual detail against the physical workload of the laser scanners.

Path Filtering & Limits

These are critical safety and optimization tools to prevent overwhelming the laser scanners with too much complex geometry.

  • Min / Max Length: Defines length limits as a percentage. Setting Min Length to 10% will automatically hide any generated polylines that are shorter than roughly 11 pixels—excellent for instantly removing visual noise from traced video.

  • Count: Defines the absolute maximum number of polylines to keep and send to the laser.
  • Mode: If the vectorization exceeds the maximum Count limit, this parameter defines which paths to prioritize and keep (e.g., Keep Longest or Keep Shortest).

Display & Monitor Diagnostics

Use the Display mode to switch the workspace preview between different stages of the rendering pipeline (e.g., Output Polylines vs. Processed Image). This helps you understand how the engine is breaking down the pixels.

The Monitor displays real-time errors and statistical information about the vectorization process. Use this panel to keep an eye on the internal math to ensure your composition isn't generating an unsafe amount of geometry for the hardware scanners to process.

3D Object Rendering for Laser

The Laser 3D surface allows you to import standard .OBJ files and project them as high-definition volumetric wireframes.

Laser 3D Settings

  • 3D Model: Select a built-in primitive shape or import your own .OBJ file. Adjust Face Culling to hide the back sides of objects, drastically optimizing laser rendering by preventing the scanner from drawing lines you can't see.
  • Texturing: Define how textures and colors map to the Object UVs.
  • Calibration: Use the Calibrate toggle and Fix Position button to accurately align the 3D rendering with real-world physical objects.

Process (For 3D Objects)

Controls the volumetric rendering output.

  • Set the Mode (e.g., Depth), and fine-tune the Sensibility and Definition to control exactly how much geometric wireframe detail is sent to the laser.

Laser Warping & Soft Edge

Mesh Warping

(Applies to Laser Quads, Lines, and Text)
An essential technique that applies a grid mesh to warp your laser output. Activate Bezier Mesh Warping to use curves to fit your laser perfectly to complex physical surfaces.

Soft-Edge

(Applies to Laser Quads)
Extremely useful when overlapping multiple laser projectors to cover a massive stage. This allows you to blend and fade the intersecting laser zones smoothly.

 

See video Soft Edge Blending Guide for more tips.

Laser Scanner (MAD Laser Scanner)

The Laser Scanner is an advanced auto-calibration tool that uses a camera to read test patterns drawn by your physical laser projector. It calculates the exact physical distortion and automatically generates a corrected mapping.

(See the Special Tools and Auto-Calibration page for detailed instructions on using the Laser Scanner).

 

Laser Visualization & Safety

Beam Preview

Under the Preferences > Project > Laser tab, you can customize the internal Beam Preview. It is important to note that this preview does not affect the physical output of your actual laser projector. However, it is an incredibly powerful feature because this simulation can be outputted onto standard video projectors or LED screens if desired, allowing you to seamlessly blend real lasers with simulated ones.

You can adjust the following parameters to customize the simulation:

  • Level: Adjusts the overall brightness and intensity of the simulated beam.

  • Beam Origin: Click and drag the node on the X/Y grid to simulate the physical placement of the laser projector relative to your output surface.

  • End Beam on path: Toggles whether the simulated beam visually stops exactly where it hits the drawing surface or continues passing through.

  • Enable Fog: Activates a volumetric atmospheric effect in the preview window, making it easier to visualize the "mid-air" trajectory of your beams.

  • Reset to Defaults: A quick button to revert all preview settings back to their standard state.

Laser Safety Zones & Masks

When working with high-power lasers, safety must be the primary concern. MadMapper allows you to configure area limitations or "safety masks" within the Laser Output menu. These masks are designed to physically block the software from drawing beams in designated unsafe areas (such as the audience or performer eye-lines).

These masks can be configured under the Outputs tab. Open Outputs, select your laser(s), and scroll down to the mask section associated with your layer. From here, you can create a final output mask that will be applied broadly to anything that passes through that specific projector's placement. If you are using multiple lasers, you may need to configure separate laser masks for each device to ensure that your laser beams are terminating in safe locations and not directly on your audience, live performers and dancers, or dangerous surfaces (flammable, reflective, etc.). When configuring your laser, ensure that these safety masks are created first and enabled so that they remain intact from the beginning to the end of your laser's operation.

However, software masks should never be your only line of defense. Most laser safety experts strongly advise using physical blocks (such as black foil or metal plating attached to the physical projector) to protect crowds and safety zones. A software crash or accidental parameter shift could bypass a digital mask, whereas a physical block guarantees the beam cannot hit a restricted area.

⚠️ CRITICAL LASER SAFETY WARNING ⚠️ High-power lasers can cause permanent eye damage, skin burns, and fire. You are strictly responsible for complying with all local, regional, and national laser safety laws in your country. Always ensure beam paths are safely terminated, use a physical safety switch (e-stop) on your hardware, and never operate without appropriate hardware safety monitoring systems engaged. Use at your own risk.

Previsualization Setup (Capture / Depence / WYSIWYG / LA.preview)

Because laser data is output via Art-Net, you can send your laser paths to 3D simulation software on the same computer to visualize your show before arming the physical hardware.

Before configuring your network, go into MadMapper Preferences > Project > Laser and check the box to enable External Visualisation. Use the dropdown menu to select your specific previsualization software: Capture, Wysiwyg, Depence, or LA.preview.

However, an issue often arises where MadMapper and the visualizer (like Capture) attempt to use the same Art-Net port (6454) on the localhost, causing a conflict. To solve this, you must create a Virtual Network Interface.

Creating a Virtual Network (macOS 14+)

On newer versions of macOS, creating a virtual interface through System Settings prompts you to select a "device interface" to combine physical network cards. Since we want a purely virtual network, you must use Terminal.

Step 1: Create the Virtual Network

  1. Open Terminal (Applications → Utilities → Terminal).
  2. Copy and paste the following command: sudo ifconfig lo0 alias 2.0.0.2 255.0.0.0
  3. Press Enter and type your Mac password (it will remain hidden while typing).
  4. Press Enter again. (Note: This Terminal command is temporary. You will need to run it again after restarting your Mac).

Step 2: Configure MadMapper

  1. Open MadMapper and go to Preferences → Project → DMX Output.
  2. Set Protocol to Art-Net.
  3. Set Network Interface to 2.0.0.2.
  4. Turn OFF Use Unicast (Output Mode must be Broadcast).
  5. Note your Start Universe (e.g., 0).

Step 3: Configure Capture

  1. Open Capture and go to Project → External Universes.
  2. Enable Art-Net.
  3. Set the Universe to 1. (Important: MadMapper's Universe 0 = Capture's Universe 1).
  4. If the connection fails, check your Mac's firewall settings to ensure Capture and MadMapper are allowed to communicate.

Creating a Virtual Network (Windows)

Step 1: Create a Loopback Adapter

  1. Open the Device Manager.
  2. Go to Action > Add legacy hardware.
  3. Select "Install the hardware that I manually select from a list (Advanced)".
  4. Choose Network adapters, then select Microsoft as the manufacturer, and choose Microsoft KM-TEST Loopback Adapter.
  5. Once installed, assign it a static IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.50, subnet mask 255.255.255.0) in your Windows Network Connections settings.

Step 2: Configure MadMapper and Capture

  1. In MadMapper, set your Art-Net output to the static IP address you just created (e.g., 192.168.1.50). Turn OFF Unicast.
  2. In Capture, enable Art-Net and match the universe numbers (Remember: MadMapper's Universe 0 = Capture's Universe 1).

MiniMad User Guide

(This is an abbreviated online example of the official MiniMad User Guide.  For a more comprehensive overview download the official guide from here) 

The MiniMad is an all-in-one dedicated media playback device for video and LED mapping, based on the Raspberry Pi platform. Easy to use, small, and versatile, it can be a reliable replacement for a computer in audiovisual installations.

MiniMad works with an SD-card that contains both the system and the software. It can either be installed with MiniMad Video to play video-mapping, or with MiniMad Light to play recorded DMX sequences.

The official MiniMad User Guide can be found online here or from the Help menu in the MadMapper Application

Note: MiniMad Video and MiniMad Light cannot be installed at the same time on the same SD-card.

Hardware & Power Management

Turning the MiniMad On

Turning the MiniMad on is as simple as plugging it in. To avoid physically plugging it in and out, you can use an AC power-switch.

Turning the MiniMad Off

Depending on the chosen export settings, you can either safely disconnect the MiniMad from power, or you may be required to shut it down properly to avoid data-corruption on the SD-card.

Data-corruption can happen if power is cut while the MiniMad is writing to the SD-card. This occurs:

  • When changing media (if the "start last played media" setting is checked).
  • When changing master luminosity or audio volume.
  • When changing the playback mode.
  • When editing using the mapping or image control modes in MiniMad Video.

If you use any of these features, do not cut the power directly. Instead, perform a proper shutdown using the MiniMad buttons (Hold Red + Blue for 2.5 seconds), a USB keyboard (Q), the MiniMad Controller, or via OSC. The green LED will blink 6 successive times to indicate the device can be safely electrically powered-off.

SD-Card Management

Activating Your SD-Card:
If you flash your MiniMad SD-card or use an SD-card from another MiniMad unit, you must activate it. Insert the card, connect an HDMI display, plug in the power, and follow the on-screen procedure. The red LED will blink rapidly when activation is required and stop once activated.

Flashing Your SD-Card:
Flashing is necessary if a newer system version is available, you are using a brand new SD-card, or the system suffers data corruption. Download the latest MiniMad system image from the MadMapper Downloads page and use the Etcher tool to flash the SD-card.

MiniMad VIDEO

Features

  • Surfaces: Supports Quad, Triangle, Circle, and Mask surfaces. (Lines, 3D surfaces, and FX are not currently supported).
  • Media: Supports a single media at a time across all surfaces. Movie files are transcoded during export to maximize smoothness. The maximum file size is 4GB (FAT32 limit) for a 16GB SD-card.
  • Projector: Supports a single projector via HDMI up to 1080p (1920x1080).

Exporting to MiniMad Video

In MadMapper, click File > Export Video Mapping to MiniMad. (FFmpeg Tools installer is required). You can either insert the SD-card directly into your computer or export over the network to a remote MiniMad.

For simple setups (like a single fullscreen quad with no color correction), MadMapper will offer to switch on Fullscreen maximum quality mode to output up to 1080p30. Note: Mapping and color correction controls are disabled on the MiniMad when this mode is active.

 

Network Synchronisation

Connect multiple MiniMad units to the same ethernet network (via a switch) to synchronize media playback automatically. Movie synchronization happens across units playing a movie with the exact same frame count and framerate. Any media-related action (pause, restart, mode change) made on one MiniMad happens instantly across all connected units.

MiniMad LIGHT

Recording & Exporting

In MadMapper, once your DMX fixtures are set up, open Tools > MadLight Recorder. Click "Start Recording" to capture your DMX output, and optionally select an audio track. You can edit the in/out frames in the sequence list.

Click Export to MiniMad. By default, MiniMad uses the same DMX interface as MadMapper, but you can select a different one. For ArtNet, sACN, or OSC control, you can choose Automatic (DHCP) or Manual network configuration.

Audio Output

MiniMad can play audio through its mini-jack connector or via an external USB system-compliant audio device. Make sure to plug in the USB audio device before powering the MiniMad on. If the audio device draws too much power, use an externally-powered USB hub.

Controls (Video & Light)

OSC & MiniMad Controller

The MiniMad listens to OSC commands on port 1111 and declares itself via Bonjour. In MadMapper, you can create a new MiniMad Controller module to get full control of the device, mapping parameters to Keyboard, MIDI, OSC, BPM, or Cues.

Hardware Buttons (Media / Light Mode)

  • Red + Blue: Hold to shutdown.
  • Up: Change playback mode.
  • Down: Pause media / Long press to restart.
  • Left / Right: Previous / Next media (or sequence).
  • Yellow + Up/Down: Control Luminosity (MiniMad Light).
  • Yellow + Red: Toggle Blackout (MiniMad Light).

 

Keyboard Controls

You can attach any USB keyboard as a remote control. Key shortcuts include:

  • Q: Shutdown
  • Space: Pause / Play
  • Numbers (0-9): Direct access to the first 10 media/sequences.
  • Arrow Keys: Navigate media, adjust luminosity, or move control points (in mapping mode).

Troubleshooting & Tips

LED Status Guide

  • Red (Solid): Powered and running normally.
  • Red (Blinking Rapidly): SD-Card requires activation.
  • Red (Blinking Slowly/Randomly): The device is not getting enough power. Ensure you are using the official 2A power supply.
  • Green (Blinking): SD-card is being accessed.

Tips and Tricks

  • Industrial Grade SD-Cards: For permanent installations or hot environments, we highly advise upgrading to Industrial/Military grade SD-cards to prevent data corruption.
  • Exporting Generators/Materials: MiniMad Video cannot natively render MadMapper Materials or Generators. To use them, record your output using Syphon/Spout, and export the resulting video file to the MiniMad.
  • Saving Modifications: No action is required to save. MiniMad automatically saves all mapping modifications when you exit the mapping mode (Red button).
  • Rebooting: You can quickly reboot the MiniMad by holding all three colored buttons (Red, Yellow, Blue) at the same time.

Technical Specifications

  • Based on Raspberry Pi 2 Model B
  • 7 buttons control panel
  • HDMI output up to 1080p60 (1920x1080 at 60Hz)
  • 16 GB MicroSD-card included
  • 2 Amps power supply (5V dc)

Audio Routing & Multi-Channel Sound Cards

Advanced installations often require complex audio setups, such as routing audio from MadMapper into a Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) like Ableton Live, or sending discrete multi-channel audio tracks from a single video file to an array of physical speakers. This section details how to configure multi-channel sound cards and virtual audio cables on both macOS and Windows systems.

Multi-Channel Video Playback

If you are playing a movie file encoded with multi-channel audio (e.g., 4.0, 5.1, or 8-channel audio), MadMapper can output all discrete channels simultaneously, provided your operating system and sound card are configured correctly.

  • macOS Configuration: macOS handles multi-channel audio routing natively. Simply open MadMapper, navigate to Preferences > Audio > Audio Output, and select your multi-channel hardware interface.
  • Windows Configuration: By default, standard Windows audio drivers (like Direct Sound) may only provide a stereo output. To enable true multi-channel support on a Windows machine, you must navigate to MadMapper's Preferences > Audio and select the ASIO driver type. (Note: ASIO drivers require exclusive access to the audio device. Ensure no other applications or Windows system sounds are currently using the sound card, or MadMapper will fail to open the driver).

macOS: Virtual Routing with BlackHole

BlackHole is a modern, zero-latency virtual audio driver for macOS that replaces older tools like Soundflower. It acts as an invisible cable, allowing you to pass audio seamlessly from MadMapper into other software.

  • Install BlackHole: Download and install BlackHole (the 16-channel version is highly recommended to ensure you have enough bandwidth for multi-channel video files).
  • Create a Multi-Output Device (Optional but Recommended): If you route MadMapper directly to BlackHole, you will not be able to hear the audio out of your physical speakers. To solve this, open the native macOS Audio MIDI Setup application. Click the + button at the bottom left and select Create Multi-Output Device. Check the boxes for both your physical sound card (e.g., External Headphones or Focusrite) and BlackHole.

  • Route MadMapper Output: In MadMapper's Preferences > Audio, set the Audio Output to either BlackHole or your newly created Multi-Output Device.

  • Receive Audio in DAW: Open your receiving software (like Ableton Live or Logic Pro), go to its audio preferences, and set the Input Device to BlackHole. You can now arm a track to receive and record audio directly from MadMapper.

Windows: Virtual Routing with JACK

The JACK Audio Connection Kit is an industry-standard, professional sound server daemon that allows you to connect a myriad of different audio applications to an audio device, and to route audio between them.

  1. Install JACK: Download the JACK installer for Windows. During the installation process, ensure that you check the box to register JackRouter. This is the crucial virtual ASIO driver that MadMapper will use to communicate with the JACK server.
  2. Start the Server: Open QjackCtl (the JACK Control panel) and click Start. The server must be actively running before you launch your audio applications.
  3. Configure MadMapper: Open MadMapper, navigate to Preferences > Audio, and select the ASIO driver type. Choose JackRouter from the dropdown list.
  4. Configure Receiving Software: Open your target software (e.g., Ableton Live or OBS) and similarly set its input driver to ASIO and device to JackRouter.
  5. Patch the Cables: Return to QjackCtl and click on Graph or Connections. This interface displays all running JackRouter applications. Simply click and drag from MadMapper's output nodes to the input nodes of your desired software or physical multi-channel sound card to establish the virtual connections.

Tip: Ensure that the sample rates (e.g., 44.1kHz or 48kHz) perfectly match across your operating system, MadMapper, your virtual router, and your physical sound card. Mismatched sample rates are the most common cause of clicking, popping, or completely dropped audio streams during a show.

Scheduling & Automation

MadMapper provides a comprehensive suite of tools for sequencing, automation, and unattended operation. By leveraging various modules and timeline features, users can establish programmable cue scheduling, rules-based logic, and calendar-based triggers using standard ICS files.

Programmable Cue Scheduling & Automation

For dynamic live performances, architectural installations, or sequenced shows, MadMapper utilizes dedicated modules to automate playback and transitions:

  • Timeline Automation: This module allows you to program complex, automated event sequences that can be looped or played back at specific times. You can create multiple Timeline Automation modules to target different timelines or cues independently.

  • Timeline Scheduler: Working alongside automation tools, the Timeline Scheduler allows you to activate specific cues or timelines on a recurring or defined internal schedule.

  • Targeting: Specifies the exact Timeline Bank and Timeline to be controlled.

  • Start & End: Allows precise trigger timing down to the Hour, Minute, and Second. It features a critical Stop on Loop End toggle to ensure playback finishes its current cycle cleanly before stopping, rather than cutting off abruptly.

  • Date Configuration: Highly customizable recurring logic allows you to set the Year and Month (to specific times or "Each" for continuous recurrence). The Day Mode (e.g., "By Week Days") offers individual toggles for Monday through Sunday.

  • Logging: The Log section provides real-time feedback when the specified Year, Month, Day, and Time matches the system clock.

Note: The automation features use a 24 hour clock.

Calendar-Based Triggers: The Calendar Scheduler Module

For robust, date-and-time specific automation, the Calendar Scheduler module allows you to trigger scenes and cues at specific dates and times from any calendar application.

Creating Schedule Events

  • Event Naming: In your favorite calendar application, create an event for each scene or cue you want to trigger, with the same name as the scene or cue. 
  • Duration: As only the starting time of the event will be interpreted, you don't need to set a specific duration. 
  • Recurrence: Recurring events (events happening on a repeating schedule) are supported. There is no limit to the number of events or date range you can import. 
  • Bank Organization: Scenes and Cues triggers you import into MadMapper are assigned to the bank of your choice. If you're using several banks, you need to create a separate calendar for each one. This way, there will be no confusion between scenes and cues sharing the same name in different banks.

Exporting and Importing the ICS File

  • Export: Once all your scenes and cues trigger events are set, export your calendar to the standard ICS format. 
  • Creation: In MadMapper, select the Modules tab, next to Outputs tab in the upper left corner. Click on the + button and create a Calendar Scheduler module. 
  • Import: Click on the Import ICS File button and select your previously exported calendar file. Alternatively, you can just drag and drop an ICS file anywhere over the MadMapper interface, and it will be imported into an automatically created Calendar Scheduler Module named after your ICS file. 
  • Offline Functionality: This process is safe: no internet connection is required.

Execution, Timing, and Conflict Rules

  • Event Preview: All the events in your calendar are imported and the 10 first events of your calendar are displayed in the Events section, showing the exact timestamps alongside the parsed event names.
  • Target Configuration: Maps the calendar events to a specific Timeline Bank and includes a Stop on Loop End toggle for smooth, cycle-completed transitions.
  • Recurrence Limits: Please note that recurring events are loaded for the next 365 days each time MadMapper project is reloaded. If your calendar includes events recurring beyond 365 days, you'll have to reload your project before the end of this time range in order for the next occurrences to be loaded. 
  • Sub-Minute Accuracy: If you need to trigger Scenes and Cues at specific times accurate to the second, you can adjust the beginning time of your events ("DTSTART") in the ICS file using a simple text editor. 
  • Conflict Resolution: Multiples iterations of Calendar Scheduler and Cue Scheduler modules can be used at the same time, allowing a wide range of scheduling possibilities. However, please keep in mind that in case of conflict between two triggers (ex: 2 different cues or scenes outputting on the same projector triggered at the same time) the last module on the list (i.e the last one interpreted) will be the one executed. 
  • Logging: The Log panel displays the file path and parsing status. It also includes a Verbose toggle for a more detailed version of the log.

Example ICS File:

BEGIN:VCALENDAR
VERSION:2.0
PRODID:-//MadMapper//Calendar Scheduler//EN
CALSCALE:GREGORIAN
METHOD:PUBLISH
X-WR-CALNAME:MadMapper Bank 1 - Projection Scenes

 

BEGIN:VEVENT
UID:b1-001@madmapper
DTSTART:20260601T170000
SUMMARY:Projector_Warmup
DESCRIPTION:Boot and calibrate all projectors before show time.
STATUS:CONFIRMED
END:VEVENT

 

BEGIN:VEVENT
UID:b1-002@madmapper
DTSTART:20260601T190000
SUMMARY:Opening_Night_Show
DESCRIPTION:Full facade projection mapping sequence. Opening night.
STATUS:CONFIRMED
END:VEVENT

 

BEGIN:VEVENT
UID:b1-003@madmapper
DTSTART:20260601T220000
SUMMARY:Projector_Shutdown
DESCRIPTION:End show and power down projectors.
STATUS:CONFIRMED
END:VEVENT

 

BEGIN:VEVENT
UID:b1-004@madmapper
DTSTART:20260605T190000
RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=FR;UNTIL=20260627T235959
SUMMARY:Weekend_Show
DESCRIPTION:Recurring Friday night projection show. Runs every Friday in June.
STATUS:CONFIRMED
END:VEVENT

 

Network Integration: The Startup Timeline Module

In addition to internal scheduling, the Startup Timeline Module provides a streamlined and dedicated way to trigger the playback of a timeline dynamically over the network or upon project launch.

  • Targeting: Allows selection of the specific Bank and the Timeline (e.g., Conductor) to be executed.

  • Delay Controls: Features precise control over execution timing, including a Time (secs) parameter for a hard delay and a visual Countdown tracker to monitor the remaining time before execution.

  • Testing: Includes a dedicated Test button to manually verify the trigger logic and network commands (such as OSC, MIDI, or DMX) before deploying the show.

For synchronized execution across a multi-machine setup, you can broadcast a single network OSC command to trigger multiple MadMapper configurations at the exact same time.

Audio Input & Beat Detection

MadMapper’s advanced audio processing engine allows you to synchronize your visual mappings and DMX lighting with live sound environments. Audio-reactive systems use beat detection and frequency analysis to drive parameters in real time. Using sophisticated algorithms to analyze the audio spectrum, you can transform simple video loops and static lights into dynamic, organic visual performances.

 

There are a number of ways to work with real-time audio inputs in MadMapper.

 

The Conductor / Timelines

If you drag an audio clip into the conductor, MadMapper will automatically analyize the audio clip and detect a BPM.

 

 

Read more about the Conductor and Timelines

 

Audio Configuration & Setup

Before mapping parameters to sound, you must route your audio signal into MadMapper’s engine.

  • Select Your Interface: Navigate to Preferences > Audio. Here, you can select your desired physical or virtual audio interface.

  • Assign Analysis Channels: Within the Audio Preferences, designate the specific "Audio Analysis Channels" you want the software to listen to. These channels act as the source for beat detection, general waveform generation, and spectrum analysis used across your project.

Global BPM & Beat Synchronization

To keep your project perfectly timed to the music, MadMapper relies on a Global BPM clock located in the Master Settings tab. This tempo can be established using several methods:

  • Audio Beat Detection: Analyzes the live incoming audio signal to automatically calculate and adjust the tempo in real time.

  • Ableton Live Link: Synchronizes MadMapper perfectly over a local network with Ableton Live or any other Link-enabled software.

  • MIDI Clock: Receives tempo data directly from external DJ hardware, drum machines, or controllers.

  • Manual Input: Allows you to manually type the BPM or use a "Tap Tempo" function to dial in the speed.

Once a solid BPM is established, you can use it to automate elements of your show. For example, if you are using the Cue Scheduler or Cue auto-play settings, you can instruct MadMapper to automatically switch to the next cue after a specific duration of beats (e.g., triggering a new look exactly every 4 or 8 beats).

 

With the Conductor > Configure Timeline Settings inspector, you can set the playback of your timeline to follow the Default speed, A set speed, the Global set BPM, or External Sync (such as Ableton live, LTC, MTC, or ArtNet).

 

Audio Analysis & Reactive Parameters

Instead of just syncing to the beat, MadMapper allows for highly granular, audio-reactive control by dividing the incoming audio into distinct frequency bands (typically Low, Mid, High, plus overall response).

  • Assigning an Audio Control: The easiest and most direct way to make a parameter react to music is to right-click on virtually any slider or widget in the MadMapper interface (such as Brightness, Contrast, or a DMX fixture's intensity) and navigate to Add Control > Audio. From the resulting pop-out menu, you can instantly assign specific audio drivers:

 

 

  • General Levels: amplitude
  • Frequency Bands: bass, medium, treble
  • Tempo & Timing: bpm, beatCount, or specific divisions like 4_beats, 8_beats, etc.

 

Refining the Reaction: Once assigned, this allows you to bind a heavy kick drum (bass) to the scale of a geometric shape, while a high-hat (treble) triggers a strobe effect on a specific LED wash.

Advanced Audio Control Settings: By opening the Control List and navigating to the Audio tab, you unlock deeper customization for how the mapped parameter responds to the audio signal:

    • Source and Target Ranges: Map the incoming audio level (Source) to a constrained or inverted parameter output (Target). For example, you can translate a standard 0 to 1 audio spike into a broader -1 to 1 visual oscillation range.

    • Filters: Apply mathematical algorithms to manage the incoming audio signal over a specified duration (in seconds). Options include Average, Weighted Average, Pulse Detection, Attack Release, and Damper. These tools allow you to prevent visual flickering, smooth out erratic volume spikes, or dial in precise peak responsiveness.

    • Curves: Toggle response curves to dictate exactly how the visual parameter scales against the audio volume. Available interpolation methods include None, Linear, Hermite, and Catmull Rom. Selecting a curve opens an interactive graph where you can add points and sculpt the exact reactivity profile, giving you ultimate control over the behavior at different volume thresholds.
